| [NOTE-828](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-828.md) v2 | Belghazi et al. — Mutual Information Neural Estimation | Mutual information is the KL divergence of the joint from the product of marginals, and its Donsker–Varadhan dual is tight exactly at the log Radon–Nikodym derivative plus a constant. Maximizing that dual over a compact family of neural critics gives an estimator that is strongly consistent, for the exact empirical maximizer, on a compact domain with Lebesgue densities, with a uniform deviation bound of order d log d/ε² in the parameter count d. The mini-batch gradient is biased; a moving average is offered as a heuristic fix without proof. | Read |
| [NOTE-830](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-830.md) | Li et al. — Self-Supervised Learning with Kernel Dependence Maximization | With image identity as a one-hot label, HSIC(Z,Y) is (Δl/N) times the gap between the mean kernel on positive pairs and on all pairs, and (1/2N²)Σ MMD²(i,j) = (N/Δl)·HSIC(Z,Y). The large-batch InfoNCE loss is exactly −HSIC(Z,Y) plus a log-mean-exp of the centred critic (eq. 28), and for a bounded kernel it bounds −HSIC(Z,Y) + γHSIC(Z,Z) up to a remainder of second order in the critic's variance (Thm B.1, whose printed remainder has the wrong sign). | Read |
| [NOTE-831](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-831.md) | Farrell & Ioannou — Generalized Stability Theory I | For a linear system du/dt = Au with A non-normal, the eigenvalues fix only the t → ∞ behaviour. Growth over a finite time t is the largest singular value of e^{At}, bounded below by the fastest mode and at t → 0 set by the numerical abscissa, the top eigenvalue of (A + A†)/2. A system with every mode damped can amplify a perturbation a hundredfold, and its forced and stochastic responses exceed those of the normal system with the same spectrum. | Read |
| [NOTE-833](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-833.md) | Sun, Shi, Liang & Li — when known classes help discover novel ones | In a spectral-contrastive augmentation graph over labelled and unlabelled data, the linear-probe residual of a novel labelling is exactly the part of it outside the top-k eigenspace that the labelled rows of the discarded eigenvectors cannot absorb. Known classes that share the novel class's attribute can make it zero, and a toy shows that known classes sharing a rival attribute make it worse. The general error bound (Theorem 5.6) is approximate and averages all known classes into one block. | Read |
| [NOTE-834](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-834.md) | Harvey, Lipshutz & Williams — What Representational Similarity Measures Imply about Decodable Information | For a linear readout that maximizes zᵀXw/M − ½wᵀG(X)w, the decoded signal is K_X z with K_X = XG(X)⁻¹Xᵀ/M, so the task-averaged agreement of two representations is Tr(K_X K_z K_Y). With K_z = I that is linear CKA, mean squared CCA, ENSD or the GULP distance, for particular G. Procrustes distance and average decoding distance bound each other only through the participation ratio of K_X − K_Y. The population limit (App. A.3) is an outline that requires b > 0 and a trace-class task covariance, and it does not reach the K_z = I case. | Read |
| [NOTE-835](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-835.md) | Grudin — Groupware and social dynamics | An argued review, not a study. Groupware fails less from technical problems than from eight social challenges, first among them that it asks extra work of members who get no direct benefit. The evidence is cases and the literature: meeting schedulers, voice annotation, project management, an abandoned issue-based system. Email succeeds because the sender who does the work is also the one who wants the message read. | Read |
| [NOTE-836](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-836.md) | Schölkopf, Herbrich & Smola — A Generalized Representer Theorem | For any nonempty set X, real positive-definite kernel k, strictly increasing g and any cost c on the training triples, even coupled, non-convex or infinite-valued, every minimizer of c + g(‖f‖) over the class F of countable kernel expansions with finite RKHS norm is a finite expansion Σ α_i k(·, x_i) at the training points. The proof uses only the reproducing property and Pythagoras. Existence of a minimizer, the extension from F to the completed RKHS, and the semiparametric Theorem 2 are not proved here. | Read |
| [NOTE-837](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-837.md) | Bach — Information Theory with Kernel Methods | With a continuous kernel normalised to k(x,x) = 1 on a compact set, the uncentred covariance operator Σ_p is a density operator. Its quantum relative entropy is sandwiched between the KL of two kernel-smoothed distributions and the KL itself, D(p̃‖q̃) ≤ D(Σ_p‖Σ_q) ≤ D(p‖q), with equality on the right only for an orthonormal, hence discrete, embedding. On the torus the gap is O(σ²) in the bandwidth. Kernel mutual information characterizes independence; conditional independence only one way. | Read |
| [NOTE-838](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-838.md) | Muandet et al. — Kernel Mean Embedding of Distributions | A survey whose load-bearing chain is short and explicit. An RKHS is a Hilbert space with bounded evaluation, so Riesz gives k_x (Thm 2.4, Prop. 2.1). If E_P√k(X,X) < ∞, the expectation functional is bounded and Riesz gives μ_P with E_P f = ⟨f, μ_P⟩ (Lemma 3.1, proved). MMD is ‖μ_P − μ_Q‖ (eq. 3.29), a metric on distributions exactly when k is characteristic. HSIC is the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the centred cross-covariance. Every result is for a fixed kernel. | Read |
| [NOTE-839](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-839.md) | Trefethen et al. — Hydrodynamic Stability Without Eigenvalues | The linearized operators of plane Couette and Poiseuille flow are far from normal. With every eigenmode decaying, perturbations can grow transiently by O(R) and resonate by O(R²), and an operator perturbation of norm O(R⁻²) makes the flow eigenvalue-unstable, all read off the pseudospectra. That transition to turbulence then follows from linear growth plus energy-neutral nonlinear mixing is a conjecture, from a 2 × 2 model. | Read |
| [NOTE-840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-840.md) | Golub & Jackson — Naïve Learning in Social Networks and the Wisdom of Crowds | Agents get independent signals with mean μ and repeatedly replace their beliefs by fixed weighted averages of their neighbours' (DeGroot). In a convergent network the consensus is s·p(0), with s the unit left eigenvector of the interaction matrix, and a growing society's limits converge in probability to μ if and only if the largest influence weight tends to zero (Proposition 2). With reciprocal, equal weights this is maximum degree over total degree → 0. A finite group that everyone attends to blocks it; balance plus minimal out- or in-dispersion guarantee it. How fast consensus is reached is unrelated to whether it is right. | Read |
| [NOTE-841](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-841.md) | Tosh, Krishnamurthy & Hsu — contrastive learning, multi-view redundancy and linear models | When two views X and Z are redundant for a label, the predictor that infers Z from X and then predicts, µ(x) = E[E[Y\|Z]\|X=x], is within εX + 2√(εXεZ) + εZ of the Bayes predictor. µ is linear in the density ratio g*(x,·) = p(x,z)/(p(x)p(z)), the optimum of the logistic contrastive problem, so m random landmark evaluations of g* support a linear predictor whose extra error falls as 1/m, scaled by a variance that is at most E[g*²] for bounded labels. Nothing requires the views to be exchangeable. | Read |
| [NOTE-842](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-842.md) | Farrell & Ioannou — Generalized Stability Theory II | For du/dt = A(t)u there are no modes, but the propagator's singular vectors and the Lyapunov exponents and vectors carry generalized stability theory over. A time-dependent operator that is stable, or neutral, at every instant can be asymptotically unstable, and only if it is non-normal. Random variation of the operator destabilizes generically, with less variation needed the more non-normal and the less damped the mean operator. | Read |
| [NOTE-843](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-843.md) | Gebhart, Hansen and Schrater — Knowledge Sheaves | A knowledge-graph embedding is a knowledge sheaf on the schema (one pair of restriction maps per relation type) with a 0-cochain of its pullback to the graph. The summed Structured Embedding score is the sheaf Laplacian form xᵀLx; adding a relation vector gives TransR, and identity maps TransE. Since the zero cochain is always a section, training needs negative triples and a margin. A multi-hop query is scored by harmonic extension, a Schur complement of the query graph's Laplacian, which beats summing TransE vectors on ip and pi queries. | Read |
| [NOTE-844](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-844.md) | Budroni, Cabello, Gühne, Kleinmann & Larsson — Kochen-Specker Contextuality | A review of Kochen–Specker contextuality. It defines noncontextual hidden-variable models minimally, as a global distribution whose marginals are the context distributions (Fine's theorem), with the sheaf, polytope, graph and hypergraph formulations called substantially equivalent. It argues that contexts need an operational definition stronger than joint measurability, which alone makes every nondisturbing correlation classically realizable. It surveys how disturbance is modelled in experiments, Kujala et al.'s maximally noncontextual models among them. Spekkens's generalized contextuality is covered only to mark the difference, and the review nowhere derives the relation between the two notions. | Read |
| [NOTE-845](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-845.md) | Balestriero, Bottou & LeCun — regularization effects are class dependent | On ImageNet with ResNet-50, making random crop stronger or changing weight decay raises mean test accuracy while some classes lose 20 points or more, and the shift survives a frozen-backbone transfer to iNaturalist. The evidence is per-class curves for hand-picked classes over 10–20 runs, plus a Welch test with no multiple-comparison correction. Theorem 1 says only that a fit to augmentations that are not label-preserving cannot equal the true function. | Read |
| [NOTE-846](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-846.md) | Tan et al. — contrastive learning is spectral clustering on a similarity graph | SimCLR's InfoNCE loss, taken over all n objects with a Gaussian kernel on the unit sphere and a symmetric augmentation matrix π, is rewritten exactly as tr(Zᵀ L(π) Z) + log R(Z): a graph-Laplacian quadratic form plus the log of InfoNCE's normalizers. The paper calls this spectral clustering under a definition that admits any regularizer. It does not show that the minimizer is a set of Laplacian eigenvectors, and it names no population optimum. | Read |
| [NOTE-847](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-847.md) | Harland — Beyond the Moral Influence Theory? | Vargas's agency cultivation model is said to differ from the moral influence theory by aiming at moral agency, but his notion of responsiveness to moral considerations is so capacious that it reduces to intrinsic motivation to act morally, so the model inherits the old theory's defects. And his counterfactual test of free will is calibrated to what makes blaming effective, so it can be applied only once we know whether blaming such agents is good policy: given the model, freedom follows blameworthiness and does no work. | Read |
| [NOTE-849](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-849.md) | Seth & Bayne — Theories of consciousness | A review of four families: higher-order, global workspace, integrated information, and reentry and predictive processing theories. Each is sorted by which aspect it explains (global states, local contents, phenomenal character, function), its anatomical commitment, and its evidence. The front-versus-back dispute is at heart a dispute over consciousness and cognitive access. Posterior-sufficiency predictions cannot now be tested because verification relies on report, which needs anterior activity, and no marker of consciousness has a validation that rests neither on introspection nor on a contested theory. | Read |
| [NOTE-850](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-850.md) | Assran et al. — The Hidden Uniform Cluster Prior in Self-Supervised Learning | MSN's entropy term is a KL penalty pulling cluster sizes toward uniform, and SwAV's Sinkhorn step enforces equal sizes outright; for VICReg the same prior is reached only through an informal reduction to K-means, and for SimCLR only by a cited equivalence. With mini-batches of two to eight ImageNet classes, SimCLR, VICReg and MSN lose 11–18 points of ImageNet linear accuracy while MAE and data2vec do not. A power-law prior in MSN gains about 1–3 points on long-tailed iNat18 and loses heavily on ImageNet. | Read |
| [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md) | Ashby — Design for a Brain | Adaptation is the stability of the organism–environment system in the region where the essential variables stay within limits. To find such stability in an unknown environment, a second feedback must change the parameters of the first whenever an essential variable leaves its limits: the ultrastable system, shown in the Homeostat. Its blind search takes time exponential in the number of variables unless partial adaptations are kept, and keeping them needs a system that is not fully joined, its parts separated by constancies. New learning destroys old to the degree that it uses the same parts. | Read |
| [NOTE-852](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-852.md) | Chuai & Zhao — Anger makes fake news viral online | On Weibo 2011–2016, lexicon-scored fake news carries more anger and less joy than true news, and in regressions with content, author and topic controls a post's share of anger words goes with more retweets and its share of joy words with fewer; the R² of the retweet models is 0.08–0.13. Two anger-dominated items in a 1,291-response survey drew slightly more anxiety-management and information-sharing motive than joy-dominated ones. The paper calls this causal; the design is observational. | Read |
| [NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md) | Fricker — Evolving Concepts of Epistemic Injustice | Fricker's later statement of her two concepts. Testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement through prejudice, and never a deliberate manipulation of credibility. Hermeneutical injustice is caused by hermeneutical marginalisation and persists despite individual good faith. Both are "discriminatory" epistemic injustice, distinct from distributive kinds. Testimonial injustice can be structural and pre-emptive, as with an un-refreshed list of expert witnesses. | Read |
| [NOTE-854](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-854.md) | Adler — Hilbert spaces and the Riesz representation theorem | An undergraduate expository proof, twice over, that every continuous linear functional on a Hilbert space is v ↦ ⟨u, v⟩ for a unique u with ‖u‖ = ‖φ‖: once from the projection theorem, once as u = Σ_k conj φ(e_k) e_k over any orthonormal basis, with ‖φ‖² = Σ_k \|φ(e_k)\|². It ends with von Neumann's proof of the Radon–Nikodym theorem for finite positive measures by applying Riesz to f ↦ ∫ f dν on L²(ν + μ). | Read |
| [NOTE-855](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-855.md) | Bra–ket notation (Wikipedia) | Dirac's notation writes vectors as kets and linear functionals as bras. On a Hilbert space the inner product, antilinear in its first slot, turns each ket into a bra, and the article cites the Riesz theorem for the reverse direction; on a Banach or untopologized space the bracket is only a functional applied to a vector, because Riesz does not apply. The article is a reference with internal inconsistencies, including an unsourced edit of 2026-09-30 to the date of the notation's origin. | Read |
| [NOTE-856](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-856.md) | De Marco and Cyr — Manipulation Cases, Part 1 | An even-handed survey of manipulation arguments. It quotes Pereboom's Case 1 and describes Cases 2 to 4, gives the generic schema (No-FR, No-Diff), and notes that Pereboom's own version concludes by best explanation. Original-design cases defeat bypassing views, and natural-force cases defeat manipulator-focused views. Hard-line replies, parallel indeterministic cases, three dilemmas against the argument, and Todd's mitigation version are set out. | Read |
| [NOTE-857](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-857.md) | Gelfand–Naimark–Segal construction (Wikipedia) | For a state ρ on a C*-algebra A, the semi-inner product ⟨a, b⟩ = ρ(b*a) on A, quotiented by its null left ideal and completed, carries A acting by left multiplication, with the class of the identity as a unit cyclic vector and ρ(a) = ⟨π(a)ξ, ξ⟩. Any two cyclic representations with cyclic vectors reproducing the same state are unitarily equivalent, by the unitary π(a)ξ ↦ π′(a)ξ′. The representation is irreducible exactly when the state is pure. The article says nothing about kernels. | Read |
| [NOTE-858](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-858.md) | McAllister & McCrea — Long-term consequences of repetitive concussion | A narrative review: almost all athletes recover clinically within 1–2 weeks of a sport concussion, but when it was written (published March 2017) no prospective longitudinal study had measured the long-term cognitive, psychiatric or neurodegenerative risk of repeated concussion or of non-concussive head impacts. The evidence for such risk, CTE included, is retrospective, case-based or survey-based and mixed, and the authors call for large prospective cohorts with controls. | Read |
| [NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md) | Fricker — Powerlessness and Social Interpretation | Hermeneutical injustice is having a significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to hermeneutical marginalisation. It is systematic when the marginalisation is persistent and wide-ranging, and incidental when it is one-off and local, which can happen to a socially powerful subject. A gap with no marginalisation behind it is bad luck. The primary harm is situated hermeneutical inequality. Secondary harms include lost epistemic confidence and the social construction of identity. | Read |
| [NOTE-860](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-860.md) | Fricker — Epistemic Injustice and a Role for Virtue in the Politics of Knowing | A hearer takes testimony critically but without inference, through a socially trained testimonial sensibility. Because that sensibility runs on stereotypes of credibility, it can carry prejudice, and then a speaker receives the wrong degree of credibility through the hearer's unintended prejudice: testimonial injustice. The corrective virtue, reflexive critical openness, is available only where the critical concepts of the time allow it. | Read |
| [NOTE-861](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-861.md) | Riesz representation theorem (Wikipedia) | On a real or complex Hilbert space every continuous linear functional φ is x ↦ ⟨x, f_φ⟩ for a unique f_φ, with ‖f_φ‖ = ‖φ‖; the map y ↦ ⟨·, y⟩ is an antilinear isometric bijection H → H*. Completeness is used only to split H = ker φ ⊕ (ker φ)^⊥. The article then defines the adjoint of a bounded operator between Hilbert spaces through this bijection, and shows it is the transpose read through the two Riesz maps. | Read |
| [NOTE-862](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-862.md) | Caruso — Skepticism About Moral Responsibility (SEP) | The SEP survey of free will skepticism. It defines basic-desert responsibility in Pereboom's words and states hard incompatibilism: compatibilism falls to the manipulation argument, event-causal libertarianism to luck, and agent-causal libertarianism to physics. It quotes Pereboom's Case 2, gives the four-case argument's structure, and says why soft-line replies are fragile. It also reports Levy's argument that historical compatibilism cannot let agents take responsibility for their constitutive luck. | Read |
| [NOTE-864](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-864.md) | Gray & Fu — Soft constraints in interactive behavior | In a simulated VCR-programming task, people with show information always available on screen still made errors that comparing against the display would have prevented. Making that information cost a mouse move and click instead of an eye movement (an estimated 1,000–1,500 ms against 500 ms) cut how often they looked it up, and most checks came right before a setting, almost none while or after setting it. The group made to memorize the information first made the fewest errors. Gray and Fu read this as non-deliberate least-effort choice among microstrategies, with memory time and perceptual-motor time weighed alike ("milliseconds matter"). The access costs are model estimates, not measured or varied parametrically. The error difference between the two on-screen conditions was not significant, the free-access look-up data come from a separate eye-tracking study of eight people, and the Memory-Test condition differed from the others in more than retrieval cost. | Read |
| [NOTE-865](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-865.md) | Dasgupta & Gershman — Memory as a computational resource | A short review arguing that memory is used to avoid redundant computation: results are stored and reused (memoization), either whole ("top-down") or as solutions to subproblems ("bottom-up"), and amortized inference and deep Q-networks are "distributed" memo-tables that generalize to new inputs. It illustrates this in mental arithmetic, mental imagery, probabilistic inference and planning, mostly with response times that flatten with practice and with biases that a cache explains (reuse of earlier inferences, choices based on stale cached values, reuse of policy fragments). It has equations for its examples but no cost model: the space–time trade-off is named, and when caching pays is listed as an outstanding question. Memory is internal throughout; retrieval cost is mentioned once, and offloading or external stores not at all. | Read |
| [NOTE-866](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-866.md) | Hansson — Logic of Belief Revision (SEP, revision of 29 July 2026) | The entry separates two ways of representing what an agent believes: a logically closed belief set, and a belief base whose elements are the beliefs "held independently of any other belief", with everything else "merely derived". Two bases with the same closure can respond differently to the same input (its Abe and Bob example), so the closure is not a sufficient state for revision; belief-set models recover the difference only by attaching a different selection mechanism to the same set. Bases avoid the Recovery postulate, keep distinct inconsistent states apart, and permit operations (external revision, semi-revision by consolidation) that collapse on closed sets. The entry does not discuss keeping reasons, sources or justification records: its only mention of truth maintenance systems is historical, and a base records which beliefs are basic, not why they are held. Iterated revision is treated as an open area in which most proposals carry an ordering of worlds or an entrenchment relation as the state, not a base. | Read |
| [NOTE-867](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-867.md) | Hutchins — How a cockpit remembers its speeds | In an MD-80 approach, the correspondence between airspeeds and wing configurations for the day's landing weight is computed once, 25 to 30 minutes before landing, by selecting a printed speed card with the displayed gross weight, and is stored in the positions of movable bugs on both airspeed indicators; when the plane slows 10 to 15 minutes later, the needle's approach to a bug cues each flap call by a judgment of spatial proximity. Hutchins argues that this memory belongs to the cockpit as a functional system and that speed bugs do not improve any pilot's memory but replace a recall-and-scale-reading task with a perceptual one. The account is a stylized description of mandated procedure, informed by more than 100 observer flights and simulator recordings, with no measured performance, no comparison of crews with and without bugs, and no failure cases; the claim that the arrangement changes what the system can do is established by analysis of the tasks, not by data. | Read |
| [NOTE-868](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-868.md) | Gray, Sims, Fu & Schoelles — The soft constraints hypothesis | In a Blocks World copying task where the model pattern was hidden and opening it cost a lockout of 0 to 3,200 ms, people opened it less often, kept it open longer, and placed more blocks after the first look as the lockout rose, and the trend was graded down to differences of tens of milliseconds. An Ideal Performer Model that chooses how many blocks to encode per look (ENCODE-1 to ENCODE-8) by Q-learning, with the only reward being negative time and memory given by ACT-R's base-level activation, retrieval-threshold and latency equations, fits four measures from Experiment 3 with three memory parameters and one softmax noise parameter fitted on one of them. The authors read this as support for choosing between head and world by time alone, against a minimum memory hypothesis, which they concede no one has stated precisely enough to model. The model's only memory costs are encoding time, retrieval time and forgetting; it has no term for anything carried across trials, for a retrieved item being wrong, or for the world changing. | Read |
| [NOTE-869](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-869.md) | Snell, Lee, Xu & Kumar — Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally | On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, which way of spending test-time compute works best (beam search against a process reward model versus best-of-N; sequential self-revision versus parallel sampling) depends on how hard the question is for the base model, and choosing the method per difficulty bin matches best-of-N with up to about 4× less test-time compute (the discussion says 2–4×). In a FLOPs-matched comparison with a ~14× larger model, the extra test-time compute a small model may spend is set by R, the ratio of total inference tokens to pretraining tokens: when R is small the larger model's pretraining cost buys many samples per query and test-time compute wins on easy and medium questions; when R is large the budget per query falls toward the parameter ratio and the larger model wins, always on the hardest questions. Difficulty estimation (2048 samples per question) and verifier and revision-model finetuning are not counted in the compute, R is an aggregate token ratio with no term for which queries recur, and the evidence is one model family on one benchmark of 500 test questions. | Read |
| [NOTE-870](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-870.md) | Geisler — Contributions of ideal observer theory to vision research | A short review, not a methods paper. It defines the ideal observer as the device that "performs a given task at the optimal level possible, given the available information and any specified constraints", writes the Bayesian ideal as an argmax of expected utility over the posterior given either the stimulus S or a constrained neural representation Z = g(S;θ) (eq. 1), and surveys applications from photon-noise detection to eye-movement search. It gives no formula for efficiency and no procedure for locating information loss beyond saying that constraints are added to the ideal one at a time (optics, receptor sampling, receptor noise, ganglion-cell summation) and that models are built by "degrading the ideal observer with hypothesized neural noise or with hypothesized heuristic computations". Its constraints restrict the information available to an optimal decoder; it has no notion of an optimum over a restricted class of computations, though its attention examples compare the ideal with specific suboptimal rules (a one-location "serial" mechanism, a MAP searcher, a random searcher). | Read |
| [NOTE-871](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-871.md) | Kirsh — The intelligent use of space | A classification, from video of cooks, assemblers and baggers, informal observation and the Tetris studies, of how people arrange things around them to cut the time and memory a task needs: arrangements that simplify choice (hide or highlight affordances, eliminate decisions, offload heuristic properties), arrangements that simplify perception (clustering, regions, marking, the vernier effect), and spatial dynamics that save internal computation (Tetris rotation, self-cueing). It frames the savings in search-complexity terms and links informational structuring to amortized computation in a footnote, but says the savings cannot in general be meaningfully quantified and offers no cost model, no measurements beyond the cited Tetris timings, and no case of an arrangement failing under a deadline. Its agents are experts arranging their own workspace in the medium and short term; long-term, pre-built environments are set aside. | Read |
| [NOTE-872](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-872.md) | Kirsh — Adapting the environment instead of oneself | A conceptual paper. It models a task as a directed graph of states and actions with a cost metric on transitions, and classifies how an agent can improve its payoff by actions external to the task: pruning hard initial states, routine maintenance, scouting ahead, tools (which change the graph), and actions that make a space more "cognitively congenial" (which leave the graph intact and reduce mental operations). It names amortization once, as a parenthetical gloss on chimps leaving nut-cracking stones in place, and gives an investment rule for maintenance (future benefit against present cost times an "interest factor" for risk) in words only. There is no cost model with reuse frequency, retrieval cost or staleness; mental cost lies outside the graph, and the paper says there is "no general theory" of congeniality. The empirical figures are unpublished pilot results. | Read |
| [NOTE-873](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-873.md) | Lieder & Griffiths — Resource-rational analysis | Resource rationality defines the right cognitive mechanism as the one, among those a brain can execute, that maximizes expected utility of its result minus the expected opportunity cost of the time and resources it uses (Eq. 3), averaged over the environments consistent with what is known (Eq. 4); resource-rational analysis is a five-step iterate-and-refine method for deriving process models from that objective. The objective is per episode. It has no separate terms for storing a result, retrieving it later, or its going stale: the value of what a computation leaves behind is folded into the utility of the episode's result, and the cost of finding the heuristic in the first place is assigned to evolution and learning and left out. Reuse appears only in the review, qualitatively: habits as reused action sequences, Dasgupta et al. 2018's memorized hypotheses, Howes et al. 2016's memorize-or-look-up trade, and "cognitive prostheses". The framework is offered as a methodological device, not a claim that people are optimal. | Read |
| [NOTE-874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-874.md) | Alchourrón, Gärdenfors & Makinson — On the logic of theory change: partial meet contraction and revision | For a logically closed theory A, the contractions satisfying Gärdenfors's six basic postulates are exactly the partial meet contractions, A ∸ x = ⋂γ(A ⊥ x), where γ picks a nonempty subset of the maximal subsets of A not implying x (Observation 2.5); adding the two supplementary postulates gives exactly the contractions whose γ is generated by a transitive relation over those subsets (Corollary 4.5). Revision is defined from contraction by the Levi identity and inherits the corresponding postulates. The result needs, besides A, a selection function or ordering that A itself does not supply: different selection functions give different contractions of the same theory, and in the finite case distinct selection functions always give distinct contractions (Observation 4.6). The setting is one-step change of a single fixed theory; nothing is said about iterated change, about where the selection function comes from, or about the reasons for which a belief is held. | Read |
| [NOTE-875](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-875.md) | Dasgupta, Schulz, Goodman & Gershman — Remembrance of inferences past | In three online experiments (N = 84, 80 and 100, before exclusions), a sub- or superadditivity bias induced in a first probability judgment carried over into a second, always-packed judgment about the same scene distribution, and errors on the two queries were correlated trial by trial (r ≈ 0.34–0.67). The carry-over appeared only when the second query shared part of its hypothesis space with the first, which rules out simple numerical anchoring; it was larger when cognitive load fell on the first query, which the authors' simulations read as reuse of a summary statistic rather than of the stored samples; and with a new cue it appeared (for subadditivity only, and weakly) when the cue's posterior was similar to the first. The paper defines amortization as reuse of past computation bought at a cost in bias, and itself places it in the time-for-space trade. It measures no response times, so the speed benefit is assumed, not shown; efficiency is shown only by better secondary-task accuracy on reusable trials; and it gives no account of when reuse pays. | Read |
| [NOTE-876](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-876.md) | Harris et al. — Failures to replicate a key result of selective accessibility | Five preregistered experiments (N = 128 each, about four times the originals' N) failed to replicate the lexical-decision result of Mussweiler and Strack (2000a, Studies 1 and 2). That result was that after a comparison with a high or low anchor, words consistent with the anchor are recognised faster. Every experiment produced a large anchoring effect on the later estimate (d ≈ 0.85–1.39), and none showed the accessibility interaction (all η²G ≤ .004). An exploratory Bayesian meta-analysis gave a Bayes factor of 21.1 for the null. Validation experiments found that the same tasks also missed direct picture priming. So the authors conclude that the method cannot detect the effect, not that selective accessibility is false. They still call the theory "a good explanation", but say the earlier lexical-decision evidence "is not a strong part of the evidence base". | Read |
| [NOTE-877](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-877.md) | Strack & Mussweiler — Explaining the enigmatic anchoring effect | In three small between- and within-subjects studies (N = 32, 32 and 67), the anchor's effect on a later estimate depended on what the comparison task brought to mind, not on the number alone. With the anchor number held fixed, the effect was large when the estimate was on the dimension compared (Study 1). It reversed to contrast when the estimate was about a very different object (Study 2). After plausible anchors, the comparison took longer and the estimate came faster (Study 3). Accessibility is inferred from these moderations and from latencies. No study measures what knowledge was retrieved. The paper also keeps an adjustment-like route for implausible anchors, which anchored at least as strongly. | Read |
| [NOTE-878](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-878.md) | Kirsh & Maglio — On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action | Kirsh and Maglio define an epistemic action as a physical action whose primary function is to reduce the space, time or unreliability of the agent's own mental computation, and argue from Tetris keystroke data that players rotate and translate pieces for that reason: zoids are rotated more than plan-then-act would need, rotation starts within a few hundred milliseconds of a zoid appearing, and a translate-to-wall check is used more the higher the drop. The computational saving is argued, not measured: physical rotation of 90° takes as little as 100 ms against an estimated 800–1200 ms mentally (a three-player pilot), and fewer attentional probes and less working memory are needed. The trade is physical action in place of internal computation at the moment of use, not precomputation or caching; the paper explicitly sets it against caching and chunking accounts of skill, and mentions amortized complexity only in passing for everyday cases such as sorting bolts before assembly. It says the choice fits a Stigler-style cost–benefit model in outline but that such models fail in detail, because an epistemic action's value depends on the particular internal computation it serves. | Read |
| [NOTE-879](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-879.md) | Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold & Rothblum — Multicalibration: calibration for the computationally-identifiable masses | A predictor is α-multicalibrated on a collection C of subpopulations if, within every set S in C, the individuals given (roughly) the same prediction v have true probabilities averaging within α of v, except on an α-fraction of S. For any C whose sets have size at least γN, a simple iterative patching algorithm reaches multicalibration from O(log\|C\|/α^{11/2}γ^{3/2}) samples in time linear in \|C\|, and the result is a circuit only O(s/α⁴γ) in size when the sets of C are computed by size-s circuits. Learning it is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to weak agnostic learning of C, so it is hard for rich C under cryptographic assumptions. Calibrating any predictor h on its own level sets as well as on C costs at most 6α in squared error. All guarantees are relative to the benchmark p*, which is itself defined relative to the features available, and they hold only for large sets; the paper offers no uniqueness for the predictor and does not state a theorem in indistinguishability form. | Read |
| [NOTE-880](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-880.md) | Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin & Luby — A pseudorandom generator from any one-way function | There is a pseudorandom generator if and only if there is a one-way function (Theorem 6.2.2), in the uniform setting: adversaries are algorithms, and every reduction is an oracle Turing machine that turns an adversary for the constructed generator into an inverter for the given function. The route runs one-way function → false entropy generator → pseudoentropy generator → pseudorandom generator, where "computational entropy" is the Shannon entropy of some P-samplable distribution that no adversary of the given strength tells apart from the output. The general reduction is only weak-preserving: composed literally it needs seeds of length n^34, and the paper's direct construction n^10. The paper attributes to Goldreich [G : 89] the equivalence of pseudorandom generators with P-samplable pairs that are computationally indistinguishable but statistically very different; with Theorem 6.2.2 that gives the one-way function form, but the paper never writes that combined sentence. | Read |
| [NOTE-881](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-881.md) | Sardana, Portes, Doubov & Frankle — Beyond Chinchilla-optimal: accounting for inference in scaling laws | Fixing a target pre-training loss and adding inference FLOPs (2N per token over a known lifetime demand D_inf) to training FLOPs (6N per token), the compute-minimising model is smaller and trained on more data than Chinchilla-optimal, increasingly so as D_inf approaches and exceeds the training-set size; the optimum has no closed form and is found numerically. The savings are modest in FLOPs (for a 30B-Chinchilla-quality model with 10^13 inference tokens, 28% by training 13.6B on 2.84× the data) and larger in dollars once inference's low hardware utilisation is priced in (17% to 58% in the paper's examples). 47 training runs (150M–6B parameters, 10–10,000 tokens per parameter) find loss still falling at extreme ratios, but more slowly than Chinchilla-fitted laws predict, so the formula overstates the gain from long training. Demand is assumed known before training and fixed given quality; there is no term for uncertainty, discounting, obsolescence or a model being replaced. | Read |
| [NOTE-882](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-882.md) | Howes, Duggan, Kalidindi, Tseng & Lewis — Short-term remembering as boundedly optimal strategy choice | Participants copied names one at a time from a mock email to a mock calendar and, after a forced phase that measured their own copying rate at every list length from 3 to 9, chose how many names to take per trial; the list length that had given each person the highest rate in their own data predicted their choice better than one item fewer or one more (55% vs 8% and 17% of choices in Experiment 1, N = 40; 46% vs 12% and 14% in Experiment 2, N = 20). An exponential points schedule raised chosen list length (6.99 vs 5.07), but doubling the cost of an error (whole trial forfeited) did not (5.00 vs 5.05). The "boundedly optimal" prediction is the argmax of each participant's measured rate, not a model with capacity, error or look-up parameters, and the task has no look-up: names are shown once, in sequence, and cannot be consulted again. 13 of 60 participants persistently chose a non-optimal length, 10 of them one item more. | Read |
| [NOTE-883](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-883.md) | Ballard, Hayhoe, Pook & Rao — Deictic codes for the embodiment of cognition | At about a third of a second, the time scale of a saccade, the article models fixation as a pointer that binds a variable in a behavioural program to a place in the world, so that what is bound is only the task-relevant feature, fetched just before use. In a block-copying task subjects looked back at the model about 1.3 times per block on average, the commonest cycle being two looks per block (one apparently for colour, one for position), and chose this slowest, lowest-memory strategy (about 3 s a block, against about 1.5 s for copying from memory) though told to be fast; separating model and copy by 70° cut looks to 1.0 per block, and one-colour patterns that could be chunked cut them to 0.7. The authors read this as working memory having a "carrying cost" that exceeds the cost of re-acquiring from the world, but that cost is inferred from the choices and never measured or modelled, and the evidence is one task with small samples (seven subjects for the main data, three for the colour-change experiment) and no statistics reported in the article. What is left in the world is unprocessed input, not a computed result, and the article argues against precomputation where the needed products cannot be foreseen. | Read |
| [NOTE-884](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-884.md) | Jones — Scaling scaling laws with board games | Training AlphaZero on Hex at board sizes 3×3 to 9×9, the best Elo reachable for a given training compute follows one change-point curve across sizes: an incline of about 500 Elo per tenfold of training compute, with the compute for perfect play rising about 7× and the compute to leave random play about 4× per added board row, and fits on small boards predicting larger ones. On 9×9 only, train-time and test-time (tree-search) compute substitute at a fixed rate: at equal Elo, each 10× of train-time compute removes about 15× of test-time compute (fit: log test = −1.2·log train + 0.004·Elo + 29), down to a one-node search, over roughly 1e14–1e16 FLOPS-seconds of training. The trade is an iso-performance curve for a single search; the paper never counts how many games or moves the trained agent will play, so it does not price amortization, and it does not state the unit of test-time compute. One game, small boards, Elo anchored to a perfect player, and no uncertainty on the fitted trade-off coefficients. | Read |
| [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md) | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum & Yona — Outcome Indistinguishability | A predictor p̃ is outcome indistinguishable (OI) relative to a class A of distinguishers when no A ∈ A can tell an individual with Nature's outcome from the same individual with an outcome drawn from Ber(p̃_i). The paper sets out four levels by how much access the distinguisher has to p̃: none, the prediction on the sampled individual, oracle queries, or the code. The lower two levels are equivalent to multi-accuracy and multi-calibration over closely related classes. At those levels OI predictors exist with size O(s/ε²), whatever Nature's complexity. At the oracle level, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some efficient distinguisher classes force any OI predictor to be nearly as expensive as Nature's own predictor. That gives a strict separation between oracle access and sample access. OI never requires p̃ ≈ p*. A predictor is good only relative to A, and with the paper's construction a weak A gives a coarse predictor that a richer A would refute. The paper covers binary outcomes, a fixed representation of individuals and single samples (multi-sample OI is left mostly to future work). | Read |
| [NOTE-886](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-886.md) | Gershman & Goodman — Amortized inference in probabilistic reasoning | Gershman and Goodman define amortized inference as the reuse of past inferences, cached as sub-computations, to answer related later queries. They report two small online experiments in which order alone made reuse available. When a sub-query came before a complex query on a five-node Bayesian network, a person's answer to the complex query could be predicted from their own answer to the sub-query (r = 0.28; r = −0.11 when the order was reversed). Answers to the complex query were also faster relative to a structurally matched baseline. Reuse in this paper is internal memory, and it is shown only through correlation and speed, within one task, with small effects. The paper does not measure costs. Storage cost and the choice of what to store are listed as open trade-offs. Bias, staleness and interference are not studied: reuse that may be "inaccurate" without modification, and interference and forgetting of stored inferences, appear only as questions. | Read |
| [NOTE-887](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-887.md) | Risko & Gilbert — Cognitive offloading | A short review that defines cognitive offloading as physical action that changes a task's information-processing requirements to reduce cognitive demand, splits it into offloading onto the body and into the world, and proposes a metacognitive model: whether people offload is a strategy choice driven by their evaluation of internal versus extended strategies, which tracks objective internal demand but can be wrong, and offloading in turn changes both memory and those evaluations. The evidence is a handful of choice/no-choice studies, summarised qualitatively; the review reports no effect sizes and no formal account of costs. It names costs (memory for offloaded content, GPS-impaired spatial memory, photo-taking impairment, automation complacency and bias, skill decay, inflated self-knowledge, a self-reinforcing drift toward external reliance). It does not frame offloading as computation reused over time, and says nothing about how often an offloaded result is used. | Read |
| [NOTE-888](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-888.md) | Athanassoulis et al. — Designing access methods: the RUM conjecture | The paper names three per-operation overheads of an access method, each a ratio to the base data alone (read, update and space amplification, each minimum 1.0), and conjectures that bounding any two forces a lower bound on the third. Its evidence is three one-line propositions about extreme designs over an integer array (a direct-address array, an append-only log, an unindexed dense array), a placement of known structures on a triangle, and a table of asymptotic I/O costs; nothing is proved, and the formal statement does not say how large the forced bound is, so as worded it is close to empty. The extremes themselves show the overheads are not symmetric: the space-minimal design is also update-minimal, and the read-minimal design keeps updates at 2.0, so the clean conflicts are read against space and update against both. Build cost appears in the table but is outside the triangle, there is no workload weighting, no time or deadline, and no cost of examining an item other than reading it. | Read |
| [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md) | Gupta — Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse | Gupta states view selection on general AND-OR view graphs as minimizing frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget. He proves greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e (about 63%) of the optimal benefit, with the budget overrun by one view or up to double, but almost all of them assume no updates. Maintenance cost enters exactly one theorem: AND view graphs (each view has one way of being computed) in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. For OR view graphs, which include Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman's data cube, the paper sets update costs aside outright, so it does not add upkeep to that problem. Maintenance is an abstract per-update charge for keeping a view consistent. Nothing prices building a view, tolerated staleness or deferred refresh, and there are no experiments. | Read |
| [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md) | Gupta & Mumick — Selection of views to materialize under a maintenance cost constraint | Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Read |
| [NOTE-891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-891.md) | Yao — Should tables be sorted? | For storing a set of n keys from a universe {1,…,m} in a table so that the membership query (is x in S?) is answered with the fewest worst-case adaptive probes, Yao proves that when the table cells may hold only keys of S or a bounded number of pointer symbols, sorted order with binary search (⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes) is optimal once m exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold N(n, p, q), whatever the arrangement rule, table size or hashing scheme. The threshold is astronomically large, and for small universes sorted order is beaten (one probe suffices for m = 3 with n = 2, and for m ≤ 2n − 2 with n > 2). The optimality also fails as soon as one cell may hold an arbitrary value from the universe: with a single extra "directory" cell, two probes suffice for m ≥ 2^{16n²}. Only query cost is counted; building the table is free and unconstrained, so the paper says nothing about the cost of arranging or about trading arrangement cost against lookups. | Read |
| [NOTE-892](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-892.md) | Idreos, Kersten & Manegold — Database cracking | Database cracking builds an index as a by-product of answering range queries. Each select partitions, in place, the part of a copy of the column that the query had to touch, so that the qualifying values lie contiguously, and records the new boundaries in a small tree; later queries touch only the pieces at the edges of their range, so per-query cost falls as the column is split into more pieces. On a 10^7-value column under uniformly random range queries, the first cracking select costs 0.38 s against 0.27 s for a scan and about 3.3 s for sort-then-search, and cumulative cost stays below sorting's until about 10^5 queries, after which upfront sorting wins. The authors claim that only ranges of past interest get organized, but every experiment uses uniformly random ranges, so that claim is not measured; there is no cost model, no rule for when a reorganization is worth making, and updates, concurrency and out-of-memory data are left as open problems. | Read |
| [NOTE-893](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-893.md) | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph & Sleator — Competitive snoopy caching | For a shared-bus multiprocessor whose caches can either keep a replicated block (and pay one bus cycle for every write to it) or drop it (and pay p to fetch it again if it is read), the paper gives counter-based on-line algorithms whose total bus cost on every request sequence is at most twice that of the best off-line algorithm, and proves that no deterministic on-line algorithm can guarantee better than 2. The rule is: drop a copy once the writes it has caused since it was last read have cost as much as refetching it. With a third option (reading or writing through without fetching) the lower bound rises to 3, and the algorithm given is 3-competitive ignoring writebacks, 4 counting them; with associative caches the bound becomes the paging ratio. The paper never names rent-or-buy or ski rental; its rent is upkeep paid on an idle copy, and its purchase is the refetch after dropping, the reverse orientation of building a bin. Costs are fixed constants, the guarantees are worst case only, and the authors call the practical significance "unclear". | Read |
| [NOTE-894](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-894.md) | Clark — Negation as failure | Clark gives a query evaluator for a data base of clauses (a Horn clause prover in which a ground negated literal ~P is taken as a lemma when the recursive evaluation of P fails on every branch) and proves it sound with respect to the completed data base: the clauses read as the if-halves of if-and-only-if definitions, plus equality axioms saying distinct names denote distinct objects. Theorem 2: if for some selection rule every branch of the evaluation tree of Q terminates with failure, then not-(exists x)Q is a theorem of the completed data base. A branch that does not terminate licenses nothing; the rule requires the search to be exhausted, which the paper calls "the exhaustive but unsuccessful search for a proof of P". The evaluator is in general incomplete (non-ground negation, a single evaluation tree, no case analysis); it is complete for allowed queries on hierarchical data bases (Theorem 4). | Read |
| [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md) | Harinarayan, Rajaraman & Ullman — Implementing data cubes efficiently | Treats a data cube's group-by queries as a lattice in which a query can be answered from any stored ancestor, prices a query at the number of rows of the smallest materialized ancestor, and chooses which views to precompute. Choosing k views to maximize the total reduction in query cost (the "benefit") is NP-complete; a greedy rule that adds the view of largest marginal benefit gets at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimal benefit, a bound that is tight, holds unchanged with query-frequency weights, and weakens to 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view takes more than a fraction f of it. The cost of building views is represented only by their size, maintenance and updates are not modelled, the data are static, and the bound is on benefit, not on query cost. On TPC-D data the greedy order reaches nearly the minimum total query time with five views and barely more space than the base view. | Read |
| [NOTE-896](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-896.md) | Bruno & Chaudhuri — An online approach to physical design tuning | An always-on index tuner for SQL Server. It keeps, for each candidate or existing index, the running sum of what each query would have saved with it (what-if optimizer estimates, with update costs counted as losses). It creates an index once that sum has risen by the index's build cost above its lowest point, and drops it once the sum has fallen by the build cost from its highest point. For one index with no space limit, the authors call this 3-competitive against the optimal schedule that knows the workload in advance. The proof only gives a workload on which the ratio approaches 3, and the paper cites no competitive-analysis work, ski rental included. The general case (many interacting indexes and a storage limit) uses heuristics with no guarantee. All costs in the experiments are optimizer estimates, on synthetic and TPC-H workloads. | Read |
| [NOTE-897](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-897.md) | Treisman & Gelade — A feature-integration theory of attention | In visual search for a coloured letter, a target that differs from all distractors by one feature (a colour, blue, or a shape, S, among brown Ts and green Xs) was found in a time almost independent of display size (positive slopes 3.8 ms/item for colour, 2.5 for shape, display sizes 1–30), while a target defined by a conjunction (green T among brown Ts and green Xs) gave linear slopes of 28.7 ms/item when present and 67.1 when absent, the roughly 1:2 ratio of serial self-terminating search; 13 sessions of practice did not make the conjunction pop out. Making the conjunction's colours and shapes harder to tell apart nearly tripled the slope but kept it linear, and a single-feature target hard to discriminate (an ellipse of intermediate size) was slow but not item-by-item serial. Even in feature search, target-absent trials were slow and grew with display size (25.1 ms/item). The displays were at most 30–36 well-spaced items on a card, with unlimited viewing; the paper argues that conjunction structure, not similarity, makes search serial, and does not model similarity. | Read |
| [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md) | Finkelstein, Schkolnick & Tiberio — Physical database design for relational databases | DBDSGN chooses, for each table, one clustered (ordering) index and a set of nonclustered indices to minimise a frequency-weighted sum of per-statement costs (access, tuple update, index maintenance) plus a weighted storage term, under an optional page limit, taking every cost from the System R optimizer's own estimates rather than an external model. Statement costs for any configuration are computed exactly from "atomic" configurations with at most one index per table (Propositions 1 and 2), so the optimizer is consulted a linear rather than exponential number of times per table; with no elimination heuristics and a full search the tool finds the optimum, but only with respect to the optimizer's estimates. The paper gives one worked example and no measurement of actual execution, and its claims that the heuristics usually find the best solutions are not backed by reported data. The model is steady-state over a period: it has no term for the one-time cost of building an index or sorting a table, so it prices upkeep against retrieval, not a one-off sort against later retrievals. | Read |
| [NOTE-899](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-899.md) | Reiter — On closed world data bases | Reiter defines the closed-world assumption (CWA) for a function-free first-order database as reasoning from DB together with the negation of every ground atom that DB does not entail, and contrasts it with the open-world assumption (OWA), under which only what DB entails is an answer. He shows that, when DB with these added negations is consistent, closed-world evaluation of any existential query reduces to ordinary (open-world) evaluation of atomic queries combined by union, intersection, difference and projection, so the negations never need to be listed. The CWA can make a consistent database inconsistent (Pa ∨ Pb yields ¬Pa and ¬Pb); consistent Horn databases, and all definite databases, stay consistent. Nothing in the paper concerns how long a search takes: non-entailment is a fixed logical relation, and the CWA's justification is stated as an assumption of total knowledge of the domain, not proved as a soundness condition. | Read |
| [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md) | Chaudhuri & Narasayya — An efficient, cost-driven index selection tool for Microsoft SQL Server | The AutoAdmin tool picks at most k indexes (single- or two-column, clustered or not) for a given workload of SQL statements, minimising the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs of those statements, with hypothetical ("what-if") indexes made visible to the optimizer by loading their statistics into the catalog. Its contribution is search efficiency: candidates are restricted to indexes in some single query's best configuration, enumeration is Greedy(m, k) (an exhaustive seed of m indexes, then greedy additions), costs of most configurations are derived from a few "atomic" ones, and two-column indexes are generated only from winning single columns. On five TPC-D workloads this cut running time to 10–24% of a baseline, with estimated-cost quality 0–7% worse, and Greedy(2, 4) matched the exhaustive optimum on four of five workloads and was within 1% on the fifth. The cost model has no build cost, no storage term and no frequency weights, the budget is a count of indexes, the workload is fixed, there is no guarantee for the greedy step, and quality is never measured by executing anything. | Read |
| [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md) | Gupta & Mumick — Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse (TKDE 2005) | The journal paper merges Gupta's 1997 space-budget results and the 1999 maintenance-budget results into one article; it adds proofs, not new problems or new guarantees. Theorem 8 (the conference Theorem 1: inverted-tree greedy on OR view graphs, at most 2S of maintenance, at least 1 − 1/e of an optimum with the same maintenance, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum exceeds S) and Theorem 10 (A* is exact on AND-OR graphs) are now proved, while Theorem 9 (the assumption-free half-density bound) is referred to Gupta's thesis. The maintenance-budget guarantee stays confined to OR view graphs, the greedy stays exponential in the worst case, and the two constraints are never combined. The only place upkeep is traded against query cost is the 1997 formulation carried over, query cost plus maintenance cost minimized under a space budget, with a guarantee only for AND view graphs in which every view is queried more often than it is updated; build cost and staleness are not modelled anywhere. | Read |
| [NOTE-902](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-902.md) | Piatetsky-Shapiro — The optimal selection of secondary indices is NP-complete | For one relation, a known mix of equality queries and updates, single-attribute secondary indexes, and a fixed upkeep charge per index on each update, choosing the index set that minimizes average transaction cost is NP-hard: minimum set cover reduces to it, each subset becoming an attribute and each element a query that any one of its attributes' indexes can answer. The paper calls the problem NP-complete but states only the optimization version, and the proof is a sketch of about half a page. Storage is not in the model; the only price of an index is upkeep on updates. A variant with off-line updates under an update-cost budget is asserted NP-complete without proof. The paper does not cite or discuss Comer 1978. | Read |
| [NOTE-903](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-903.md) | Sleator & Tarjan — Amortized efficiency of list update and paging rules | For a list searched sequentially from the front, where reaching the i-th item costs i, moving each accessed item to the front costs at most twice what any other rule costs on the same sequence, including rules that know the whole sequence in advance (four times, counting move-to-front's own moves), with no probabilistic assumption. A fixed list sorted by access frequency, and the transpose and frequency-count rules, are not within any constant factor of that. Rearranging ahead of need never pays in this model (Theorem 3). For paging, where only a small fast memory is cheap, no rule that cannot see the future can do better in the worst case than n/(n − n_MIN + 1) times the offline optimum MIN, and LRU and FIFO attain that bound up to an additive n_MIN; with equal memories the ratio is the memory size. The model is a single linear list (or a two-level memory) with uniform items and access cost depending only on position; it says nothing about partitions, bins or search that is not a scan. | Read |
| [NOTE-904](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-904.md) | Dar, Franklin, Jónsson, Srivastava & Tan — Semantic data caching and replacement | A client cache described by the selection predicates of past queries can answer a new selection query partly from cache (the probe query, Q ∧ V) and fetch only the rest from the server (the remainder query, Q ∧ ¬V), and can evict by semantic region rather than by page or tuple. In one simulator, one client and one server, read-only selection queries on a single 10,000-tuple relation, this matched page caching on a clustered index, beat it heavily when clustering was bad, answered over 60% of small queries on an unindexed attribute with no server contact, and let a value function based on semantic distance beat LRU on a skewed workload. No replacement rule won everywhere: on regular cyclic paths MRU was best. Everything is measured, nothing is proved; updates, joins, and the CPU cost of reasoning about cache contents were not modelled. | Read |
| [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) | Indyk & Motwani — Approximate nearest neighbors: towards removing the curse of dimensionality | Approximate nearest-neighbour search in d dimensions reduces, with small overhead, to a decision problem (is there a point within r, or none within (1+ε)r), and that decision problem is solved by locality-sensitive hashing: if hash functions make near pairs collide with probability at least p1 and far pairs with at most p2, then n^ρ random hash tables with ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) answer queries with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, with constant success probability. For Hamming space by bit sampling, and for ℓ_p with p in [1, 2] by embedding, ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in the 1999 text (1/ε, for ε > 1, in STOC). The paper also gives the other end of the trade: Õ(d) query time for n·O(1/ε)^d or (nd)^{O(1)} preprocessing. It is an upper bound only: it proves no lower bound, does not claim its exponents are best, solves only the approximate problem with constant probability, and counts preprocessing as space. | Read |
| [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md) | Cho & Garcia-Molina — Synchronizing a database to improve freshness (SIGMOD 2000) | For a local copy of N items, each changing as an independent Poisson process with a known rate and refreshed at fixed intervals under a fixed total refresh rate, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy fresher and younger on average than refreshing in proportion to change rate, under any distribution of rates (proved in the technical report by convexity). The freshness-optimal allocation is neither: it rises and then falls with change rate, and gives no refresh at all to items that change too fast for the budget, while the age-optimal allocation rises slowly with change rate. On estimates from 270 web sites, proportional, uniform and optimal refresh give freshness 0.12, 0.57 and 0.62. Every item matters equally, staleness is a time average with no access or query model, the refresh budget is fixed rather than priced, and refresh, change and its detection are free of any other cost. | Read |
| [NOTE-907](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-907.md) | Chandra & Merlin — Optimal implementation of conjunctive queries in relational data bases | Defines conjunctive queries (existentially quantified conjunctions of atoms, no equality, constants naming distinct elements) and proves that two are equivalent exactly when there are homomorphisms each way between their natural models (Lemma 13). Every conjunctive query has a minimal equivalent query, unique up to isomorphism, reached by folding (Theorem 12), and that minimal query yields an evaluation program within a constant factor of optimal in the paper's cost model (Theorem 16). The hardness results are that evaluating a boolean conjunctive query on a database is NP-complete when the query is part of the input (Theorem 7), and that deciding whether one query is a folding of another is NP-complete (Theorem 11). The paper does not state a containment theorem or the NP-completeness of containment or equivalence as such; both are standard corollaries of Lemma 13's proof and Theorem 11's construction, and later papers cite them to it. | Read |
| [NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md) | Labrinidis & Roussopoulos — WebView materialization | For a page built from database queries, the paper compares three ways to serve it on a server with online updates: compute it on each request (virt), store the query result in the DBMS and refresh it on every update (matdb), or store the finished page as a file at the web server and rewrite it on every update (matweb). It gives a cost model summing access and update costs by their frequencies and states the selection problem (choose a policy per page to minimize mean response time, no space limit, no staleness allowed), but gives no algorithm for it. On one Apache/Informix testbed with cheap indexed queries, matweb answered 10 to 230 times faster than the other two at all loads tried, and matdb was slower than virt whenever there were updates, because reading the stored result cost about as much as recomputing it. Staleness is defined as the delay from update to reply, sketched, and never measured; build cost and storage are outside the model. | Read |
| [NOTE-909](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-909.md) | Levy, Mendelzon, Sagiv & Srivastava — Answering queries using views | For conjunctive queries and views, a view can be used in an equivalent rewriting of a query exactly when there is a containment mapping (a homomorphism of bodies) from the view into the query, so every possible use of a stored view is found among those mappings. Without comparison predicates, a minimal rewriting needs no more literals than the query and no new variables, which puts the search in NP; deciding whether some rewriting uses a given set of views (with comparisons only in the query), whether a rewriting with fewer than k literals exists, and whether a rewriting using only the views exists are each NP-complete, and with comparisons in both query and views existence is Π2p-complete. The hardness has two independent sources, the number of mappings and the choice of which query literals to drop, and a polynomial algorithm removes the redundant literals for a given mapping, exactly under stated conditions. Only equivalent rewritings are studied; contained rewritings, the cost of the resulting plan and the size of view collections are outside it. | Read |
| [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md) | Indyk & Xu — Worst-case performance of popular approximate nearest neighbor search implementations | For DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" graph (each point linked to the points that survive α-pruning of all other points, naively O(n³) time), greedy search from any start with no backtracking reaches a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps, each costing O((4α)^d log ∆) for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by log n. For DiskANN with its practical "fast preprocessing", HNSW, NSG and seven other graph indexes, the paper constructs two-dimensional point sets (constant doubling dimension) on which, in experiments with the authors' code at the authors' recommended parameters, the search queue must hold about 10% of the points before recall@5 becomes non-zero or the approximation ratio becomes reasonable. The linear lower bounds are empirical, for one query per constructed instance, with an informal Ω(n/R) argument for fast-preprocessing DiskANN; no theorem bounds HNSW or NSG. | Read |
| [NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md) | Labrinidis & Roussopoulos — Balancing performance and data freshness in web database servers | The paper poses Online View Selection for a web server whose database takes updates while serving requests: choose, as the workload runs, which page fragments (WebViews) to keep stored and refreshed on every update and which to cache and invalidate, so as to minimize mean response time while the fraction of fresh fragments served (QoD) stays above a threshold θ. Its algorithm, OVIS(θ), estimates per fragment the response-time and QoD change of switching, and periodically switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments greedily, spending a QoD surplus on speed or buying back a deficit; it materializes everything when it detects backlog. Nothing is proved: optimality of the greedy step is asserted, and the evidence is one synthetic simulation with fixed costs, in which OVIS kept QoD near θ, answered faster than caching alone, and recovered from overload. Upkeep and query savings share one cost, but staleness is a constraint set by the user, not a priced term, and build cost, switching cost and storage are absent. | Read |
| [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md) | Olston, Loo & Widom — Adaptive precision setting for cached approximate values | Olston, Loo and Widom set the width of each cached interval adaptively to minimize total refresh traffic. A narrow interval is escaped often (value-initiated refreshes, cost C_vr); a wide one is too imprecise for queries more often (query-initiated refreshes, cost C_qr). Under a model in which these probabilities go as 1/W² and W, the expected cost rate is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr, ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and a rule that widens on value-initiated and narrows on query-initiated refreshes, with probabilities set by ρ, reached within 1% to 5% of the best fixed width in simulation. That the rule converges is argued, not proved. With exact copies required it matched an adaptive exact-caching algorithm, and where imprecision was allowed it beat it. Staleness is priced as refresh traffic only: there is no build cost, no cost of a wrong answer, and the interval is never wrong. | Read |
| [NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md) | Green, Karvounarakis & Tannen — Provenance semirings | Annotating each input tuple with an element of a commutative semiring, and computing union and projection with + and join with ·, gives one positive relational algebra (RA+) that is set semantics over the Booleans, bag semantics over the naturals, c-tables over positive Boolean expressions, event tables over sets of outcomes, and lineage over sets of tuple ids. The polynomials N[X] in the tuple ids are the most general such annotation: for any RA+ query and any commutative semiring K, the K-annotated answer is the provenance polynomial evaluated at the input's K-annotations (Theorem 4.3). For datalog the paper needs ω-continuous semirings and formal power series N∞⟦X⟧, with the analogous factorization (Theorem 6.4) and a criterion for infinite coefficients (Theorem 6.5). Everything is positive: no negation, difference or aggregation, and revaluing inputs can only remove output tuples, never add them; trust and deletion propagation are not treated. | Read |
| [NOTE-914](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-914.md) | Panigrahy, Talwar & Wieder — Lower bounds on near neighbor search via metric expansion | Cell-probe lower bounds for near-neighbour search follow from the expansion of the graph joining points within distance r: a deterministic t-probe structure with m cells of w bits must have (mwt/n)^t at least the vertex expansion, and a randomized one must have m^t w/n at least the robust expansion at measure 1/m^t, on random data sets with weakly overlapping neighbourhoods. For the hypercube this recovers known bounds and gives, for example, space n^{1+Ω(1/(ct))} for approximation c and n^{Ω(1/(tε²))} for 1 + ε; for symmetric (Cayley) graphs a one-probe structure matches the bound, and for dynamic low-contention structures the update time must be at least the robust expansion over poly(t). The bounds are average case, for approximate decision search, and weak in t: they fall off exponentially in the number of probes, so they are tight only for a constant number of probes and say little about structures that probe n^ρ cells. | Read |
| [NOTE-915](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-915.md) | Gupta, Mumick & Subrahmanian — Maintaining views incrementally | Two algorithms compute the changes to a stored derived relation (a view) from changes to the base relations, without recomputing it. Counting stores, for each derived tuple, the number of its derivations and propagates signed counts through delta rules stratum by stratum; it is stated correct for nonrecursive Datalog or SQL views with stratified negation and aggregation, under set or duplicate semantics, and is argued to cost little beyond evaluating the view. DRed (delete and rederive), for recursive views under set semantics only, deletes an overestimate of what a deletion invalidates, puts back those tuples that still have a derivation from what remains, then adds what insertions derive; it is stated to yield exactly the tuples derivable from the new base. The paper is an extended abstract: the theorems are stated without proof (proofs are referred to a 1992 AT&T report), cost claims are argued, not measured, and there are no experiments. | Read |
| [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) | Malkov & Yashunin — Hierarchical navigable small world graphs for approximate nearest neighbour search | HNSW is a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data. Each element's top layer is drawn from a geometric distribution, and new neighbours are chosen by a pruning rule that favours diverse directions. Searching from the sparse top layer down makes per-query cost grow about logarithmically with N on uniform random data in 4 and 8 dimensions, which flat NSW graphs did not. The logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded mean degree, which HNSW does not build. For the graphs it does build, logarithmic scaling is measured, at low dimension only, and on 200M SIFT vectors the paper reports the scaling "deviates from the pure logarithm". The neighbour-selection rule is what keeps clustered data searchable: in the paper's synthetic test with 100 isolated clusters, linking each element to its nearest neighbours fails to reach high recall. There is no worst-case or recall guarantee, no deletion, and no analysis of query distributions unlike the data. | Read |
| [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan & Shaft — When is "nearest neighbor" meaningful? | For a fixed number n of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance, divided by its mean, goes to zero as dimension m grows, then the farthest point is, with probability tending to one, within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest (Theorem 1). The condition holds for IID dimensions and for several correlated or non-identical workloads, and fails when data and queries lie on a low-dimensional subspace or when queries fall inside well-separated clusters. Simulations put the collapse of contrast within 10 to 20 dimensions for IID data, and two real image-feature sets showed weak contrast. The condition is sufficient, not shown necessary; the theorem is about the ratio of distances with n held fixed, and says nothing about real data of low intrinsic dimension except that such data can escape it. | Read |
