One Bush–Mosteller learner with payoffs in (0, 1), Cross's model, moves in expectation as a population under the discrete replicator step, and in the continuous-time limit follows the Taylor replicator dynamic at any finite time. For every learning speed, though, the discrete process is absorbed in a pure strategy profile with probability one. With negative payoffs a probability-matching force enters beside a replicator force. Proofs are by Euler's method and Norman's theorems on slow learning; the negative-payoff limit is stated with its proof omitted. | Read |
| [NOTE-1150](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1150.md) | Foerster et al. — Learning with opponent-learning awareness | A LOLA learner maximises its return after the opponent's anticipated naive gradient step and differentiates through that step, adding a second-order term to its gradient. Two exact-gradient LOLA learners reached tit-for-tat-like reciprocity in the memory-one iterated prisoner's dilemma where naive learners ended at mutual defection, and settled at the mixed equilibrium of iterated matching pennies where naive learners did not converge. A policy-gradient version cooperated in the Coin Game, less reliably with a learned model of the opponent. | Read |
| [NOTE-1151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1151.md) | Leibo et al. — Multi-agent reinforcement learning in sequential social dilemmas | A descriptive simulation study. It defines sequential social dilemmas, Markov games whose learned cooperative and defecting policies give social-dilemma payoffs, and runs independent deep Q-learners on two two-player games. Scarcity and costly conflict produce aggression in Gathering; group benefit produces joint hunting in Wolfpack; and network size moves defection in opposite directions in two games that both embed a Prisoner's Dilemma. | Read |
| [NOTE-1152](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1152.md) | Foerster et al. — Counterfactual multi-agent policy gradients | A centralised critic Q(s, τ, u) trains decentralised actors, and each agent's action is scored against the critic's average over its own alternatives under its own policy, the others' actions fixed. The baseline does not change the expected gradient. On StarCraft micromanagement with a narrow field of view it beat independent and central-V/QV actor-critics on four maps. The counterfactual is the critic's estimate, not a simulation, and it values alternatives the agents sometimes take. | Read |
| [NOTE-1153](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1153.md) | Wolpert & Tumer — Optimal reward functions in distributed reinforcement learning | Members of a collective each run a reinforcement learner on a private utility, and the designer wants the world utility G maximised. A private utility is factored when it orders a member's own alternatives, others fixed, as G does; this holds exactly when it is an increasing function of G given what the member cannot affect. The Wonderful Life Utility, G minus G with the member's effect set clamped, is factored and easier to learn than G. In a 60-agent bar problem, clamping to the average action did best, clamping to absence nearly as well, G worst. | Read |
| [NOTE-1154](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1154.md) | Rashid et al. — QMIX: monotonic value function factorisation | Per-agent values Q_a(τ^a, u^a) are combined into a joint Q_tot by a mixing network whose weights, generated from the state, are kept non-negative, so ∂Q_tot/∂Q_a ≥ 0. Then the individually greedy actions form a greedy joint action and agents can act on their own values. It represents more than a sum and learned the optimum of a two-step game that a sum misses; it cannot represent a joint value in which one agent's best action depends on the others' current actions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1155.md) | Balduzzi et al. — Re-evaluating evaluation | A methods paper with two short applications. It reads evaluation data as antisymmetric matrices. Elo is then the row mean of the log-odds, exact when they are curl-free and movable by copies, and the Schur decomposition gives a multidimensional Elo. Nash averaging scores agents and tasks against the maximum-entropy Nash equilibrium of a zero-sum meta-game. Its proved invariance covers exact copies, and only when that equilibrium is unique. A checked counterexample shows what happens otherwise. | Read |
| [NOTE-1156](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1156.md) | Omidshafiei et al. — α-Rank: multi-agent evaluation by evolution | A methods paper with theory and applications. Agents are ranked by the stationary distribution of a finite-population, rare-mutation Fermi imitation chain on pure profiles, unique at every finite α. As α grows its transitions become those of Markov-Conley chains, the sinks of the better-response graph, which the paper ties to chain components of the replicator flow. The limit of the ranking is not characterized, and it is not invariant to copies. | Read |
| [NOTE-1157](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1157.md) | DeGroot — Reaching a consensus | A group whose members each replace their opinion, over and over, by a fixed weighted average of everyone's current opinions, F⁽ⁿ⁾ = PⁿF, is a Markov chain run on opinions. It reaches a consensus from every start exactly when the chain has one closed class and that class is aperiodic. The consensus is then a linear opinion pool whose weights are the chain's stationary vector, which gives members outside the closed class no weight. Two closed classes, or one periodic class, give no consensus. The weights are fixed, and nothing in the model tracks the truth. | Read |
| [NOTE-1158](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1158.md) | Bar-Tal, Yariv, Lipman and Dekel — MultiDiffusion | A training-free sampler that runs one pre-trained diffusion model on several crops or masked prompts of one canvas and, at every step, replaces their disagreeing proposals with the least-squares reconciliation, which for pixel-sampling maps is a per-pixel weighted average. It makes seamless panoramas (crop FID 10.3 against 18.4 and 45.5 for outpainting baselines) and follows rough region layouts (COCO IoU 0.26 against 0.16–0.17), most of the layout gain coming from an early masked bootstrapping phase. Its guarantee that each crop follows the reference model's path holds only at zero loss, which disagreeing overlaps do not reach. | Read |
| [NOTE-1159](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1159.md) | Kwon and Perchet — Blackwell approachability with partial monitoring: optimal convergence rates | Approachability of a polytope (reduced to the negative orthant) under partial monitoring, where the decision maker sees only a random signal whose law is known, can be achieved at rate O(T^-1/3) in expected distance for general signals and O(T^-1/2) when the signal law does not depend on the decision. The general algorithm lifts the problem to an auxiliary full-information approachability problem that is linear in the flags, and keeps a uniform exploration floor γ ∝ T^-1/3 so that the flags can be estimated by importance weighting. | Read |
| [NOTE-1160](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1160.md) | Zhong et al. — Multi-LoRA composition for image generation | Two training-free ways of using several LoRAs in one diffusion sampler without merging their weights: LoRA Switch gives each LoRA its own denoising steps in rotation, and LoRA Composite averages every LoRA's guided noise prediction at every step. On 480 sets of two to five public LoRAs, GPT-4V's paired judgements (and two annotators on 120 images) prefer both to weight merging, increasingly as LoRAs are added. In Switch, the switching interval and which LoRA acts first change the result at equal step shares. The baseline's merged adapter grows with the number of LoRAs, which the design does not separate from the decoding-time idea. | Read |
| [NOTE-1161](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1161.md) | Chaloner and Verdinelli — Bayesian experimental design: a review | Bayesian experimental design is Lindley's decision problem: choose the design that maximizes the expected utility of the best terminal decision, so the criterion follows from what the experiment is for. In the normal linear model Shannon information gives Bayes D-optimality, det(nM + R), and quadratic loss gives Bayes A-optimality, tr A(nM + R)^-1. E- and G-optimality have no utility behind them. In nonlinear problems the criteria are normal approximations that average a local criterion over the prior. Locally optimal design is the point-mass case, and it can leave the quantity of interest inestimable. | Read |
| [NOTE-1162](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1162.md) | Lattimore and Szepesvári — Cleaning up the neighborhood: a full classification for adversarial partial monitoring | Completes the classification of finite partial-monitoring games against oblivious adversaries to every game, degenerate and duplicate actions included: 0 with no neighbouring pair, Θ̃(√n) locally observable, Θ(n^2/3) globally but not locally observable, Ω(n) otherwise. The missing piece is NeighborhoodWatch2, which redistributes probability onto degenerate actions in proportion to the neighbours they lie between and has a high-probability √n bound. It corrects Bartók et al.'s T^2/3 lower-bound proof, whose separating direction ignored the degenerate actions' signals. The preprint, not the published text, also says the earlier localisation argument exchanged an expectation and a maximum. RelExp3 gives point-locally observable games an asymptotic constant depending only on K_loc, F and log K, and a factor linear in F is shown to be necessary. | Read |
| [NOTE-1163](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1163.md) | Isaac — Phenomenal structure: what is it and what is it for? | A structuralist programme for the science of phenomenal experience, set out as a stance and not a thesis. Experience has three layers of structure: quality-space geometry, which is a precondition for meaning; group-theoretic constancy, which "induces a distinction between subject and object"; and dynamic structure, vector fields of valence and affordance, which guide action. The method is the search for structure-preserving maps among experience, world and brain, held as a regulative ideal and advanced by de-idealizing the models where the maps fail. The evidence that such models target experience, not mere behaviour, is chiefly convergence between models built by different behavioural routes, which the paper admits is always partial. The group-theoretic and dynamic layers are, in the author's words, "mere suggestive sketches". | Read |
| [NOTE-1164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1164.md) v2 | Bartók, Foster, Pál, Rakhlin and Szepesvári — Partial monitoring: classification, regret bounds and algorithms | For finite partial-monitoring games the minimax regret takes exactly four rates: 0 with one non-dominated action, Θ̃(√T) when every pair of neighbouring actions is locally observable, Θ(T^2/3) when the game is globally but not locally observable, and Θ(T) otherwise. The conditions are linear algebra on loss and signal matrices: a loss difference must lie in the span of the row spaces of the signal matrices of the actions allowed to estimate it. The stochastic classification covers every game; the adversarial one covers non-degenerate games only. | Read |
| [NOTE-1165](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1165.md) | Wald — Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses | Defines the sequential probability ratio test: sample until the likelihood ratio of two simple hypotheses leaves an interval (B, A). Exact inequalities tie A and B to the error rates, so A = (1 − β)/α and B = β/(1 − α) are set with no distribution theory, and the realized errors can rise above α or β only slightly. It derives the operating characteristic and the expected sample size. It proves that no test with the same errors needs fewer observations on average under either hypothesis, once the overshoot of the boundaries is neglected, and for a normal mean it saves about half the fixed-sample test. It never mentions diffusion or Brownian motion. | Read |
| [NOTE-1166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1166.md) v3 | Meng, Bau, Andonian and Belinkov — Locating and editing factual associations in GPT | Causal tracing restores one clean hidden state into a run whose subject tokens were noised, and measures how much of the correct object's probability comes back. In GPT-2 XL, over 1000 known facts, the effect concentrates at two sites: middle layers at the last subject token, where MLP outputs dominate, and late layers at the last token, where attention does. A rank-one update of one middle MLP's output matrix, keyed on the subject's last token, then inserts counterfactual facts that generalize to paraphrases while sparing neighbouring subjects, which no other editor tested does on the new CounterFact dataset. The authors read this as showing where and how facts are stored. | Read |
| [NOTE-1167](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1167.md) | Wang, Variengien, Conmy, Shlegeris and Steinhardt — A circuit for indirect object identification in GPT-2 small | A circuit of 26 attention heads in seven classes that carries GPT-2 small's indirect-object predictions on fifteen templates, found by tracing back from the logits with path patching and checked against three criteria. Mean-ablating everything else keeps 87% of the logit difference; knocking out the three main name movers costs 5%, because other heads take over; and a greedy search finds knockouts under which circuit and model differ by up to 87%. Its by-products: heads that communicate positions rather than tokens, induction heads doing a different job from their original one, and heads that write against the answer. | Read |
| [NOTE-1168](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1168.md) v2 | Chan, Garriga-Alonso, Goldowsky-Dill, Greenblatt et al. — Causal scrubbing | A method for testing a stated mechanistic hypothesis about how a network produces a behaviour on a dataset. The hypothesis maps an interpretable computational graph into the model's graph; every activation is then replaced, recursively from the output, by its value on another input the hypothesis says is equivalent, and unclaimed inputs by their values on a random input. The share of the behaviour that survives is the score. It is applied to a parenthesis-balance classifier (93% down to 72% as the hypothesis is made more specific) and to induction in a two-layer attention-only model (35% for the naive hypothesis, 86% refined). | Read |
| [NOTE-1169](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1169.md) | Mueller, Geiger, Wiegreffe, Arad et al. — MIB, a mechanistic interpretability benchmark | A benchmark for two kinds of mechanistic-interpretability method, with fixed counterfactual inputs, private test sets and new metrics. In circuit localization, edge attribution patching with integrated gradients does best on average and node-level circuits poorly; in causal-variable localization, supervised distributed alignment search gives the highest interchange-intervention accuracy, and features of public sparse autoencoders selected by a learned mask never beat the same mask on the model's own hidden dimensions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1170](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1170.md) | Conmy, Mavor-Parker, Lynch, Heimersheim and Garriga-Alonso — Towards automated circuit discovery (ACDC) | Names a three-step workflow behind manual circuit discovery (choose a behaviour, metric and dataset; choose the units of the computational graph; patch activations to prune the graph) and automates the third with ACDC, which visits nodes from the output back and removes each incoming edge whose replacement by its value on a corrupted input raises the KL divergence from the full model by less than a threshold. Against circuits reported by earlier manual work it ranks edges with AUCs of 0.85–0.98 on three language-model tasks, beating two adapted pruning methods there, but does poorly on compiled tracr programs unless zero activations are used, misses negative components at sparse thresholds, and keeps only one input of an OR gate. | Read |
| [NOTE-1171](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1171.md) | Thibaux and Jordan — Hierarchical beta processes and the Indian buffet process | The beta process BP(c, B0) is the de Finetti mixing measure of the Indian buffet process: by beta–Bernoulli conjugacy, customer n + 1 takes dish j with probability m_{n,j}/(c + n) and Poisson(cγ/(c + n)) new dishes, which is the IBP at (c, γ) = (1, α) and its two-parameter generalisation otherwise. A hierarchy of beta processes lets groups share features, which requires a discrete shared base, at group-specific prevalences Beta(c_j b, c_j(1 − b)). On one unbalanced 20 Newsgroups split it beats tuned Laplace-smoothed naive Bayes, 58% against 50%. | Read |
| [NOTE-1172](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1172.md) v3 | Griffiths and Ghahramani — The Indian buffet process: an introduction and review | Derives the Indian buffet process as the K → ∞ limit of a finite beta–Bernoulli model, πk ~ Beta(α/K, 1), on left-ordered equivalence classes of binary matrices: the number of occupied features K+ is Poisson(αH_N) and each object holds Poisson(α) features. For finite K the paper gives only the bound E[1ᵀZ1] = Nα/(1 + α/K) ≤ Nα; the αH_N count holds in the limit, and at finite K the expected count is strictly below it. It reviews applications, the two-parameter, stick-breaking, beta process, Markov and phylogenetic variants, and names column independence as an assumption later relaxed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1173.md) | Olsson et al. — In-context learning and induction heads | In 34 transformer language models, in-context learning (loss at token 500 minus loss at token 50) appears abruptly in one early window of training, together with induction heads, the only non-convex bump in the loss curve and a turn in the models' per-token-loss trajectory; one-layer models show none of it. Letting one layer express induction (smeared keys) moves the jump, and ablating induction heads removes nearly all in-context learning in small attention-only models. The case is causal for small attention-only models and correlational or by analogy for large models with MLPs, as the authors grade it themselves. | Read |
| [NOTE-1174](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1174.md) | Dunefsky, Chlenski and Nanda — Transcoders find interpretable LLM feature circuits | A transcoder replaces one MLP sublayer with a wide sparse ReLU MLP trained on its input–output pairs. With attention patterns frozen and LayerNorm linearized, the attribution between two transcoder features factors into the earlier feature's activation times the input-invariant dot product of its decoder with the later feature's encoder, so circuits through MLPs can be read partly off the weights. On GPT2-small, Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B transcoders sit on or above the SAE sparsity–loss frontier, under one learning rate and one seed; in nine blind case studies on GPT2-small the method recovered the feature's meaning in five, mostly in two and failed in two. | Read |
| [NOTE-1175](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1175.md) v2 | Williamson, Orbanz and Ghahramani — Dependent Indian buffet processes | Couples IBPs over a covariate by thresholding Gaussian processes: z_nk(t) = 1 when h_nk(t) falls below the b_k quantile of its marginal, with stick-breaking sticks b_k that do not depend on t. Each item's indicator is then Bernoulli(b_k) at every t, so prevalence is fixed and persistence is set apart from it by the GP covariance. The paper says Z(t) is IBP-distributed at each t; that holds exactly in its collapsed model, while with a shared feature-level GP the items at one t are correlated and fewer features are occupied. Truncated Gibbs with HMC; lower held-out RMSE than the IBP on two datasets. | Read |
| [NOTE-1176](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1176.md) | Blei, Griffiths and Jordan — The nested Chinese restaurant process and hLDA | The nCRP puts a prior on infinitely deep, infinitely branching trees as a nested sequence of CRP partitions, exchangeable in its customers. In hLDA each document is one root-to-leaf path and spreads its words over that path's topics by a GEM draw, so general topics settle near the root and documents share topics only as shared ancestry. A collapsed Gibbs sampler finds an approximate posterior mode. It recovered eight of ten simulated three-level trees exactly, gave readable hierarchies of JACM, Psychological Review and PNAS abstracts, and beat LDA in held-out likelihood near its own topic count on JACM, by a harmonic-mean estimate. No identifiability result is given: the authors say recovery depends on data size and "how identifiable the topics are". | Read |
| [NOTE-1177](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1177.md) | Musat, Pimentel, Zucchet and Hofmann — Invariant learning dynamics of transformers in inductive reasoning tasks | For a class of "block-list" next-token tasks that includes associative recall, k-hop induction and in-context n-grams, population gradient descent keeps an attention-only transformer's merged key–query and output weights in a subspace fixed by the data's token-relabelling and position-shift symmetries, whose coordinates are elementary actions ("attend to the previous position", "read the token retrieved by head 1"). On it, a saturated in-weights circuit suppresses the in-context circuit's gradient by the fraction of data it does not solve, burstiness multiplies that gradient, initialization decides which of several induction circuits wins, and projecting a trained model onto the coordinates recovers its circuit, with "aiding" directions a head-level analysis would miss. | Read |
| [NOTE-1178](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1178.md) | Templeton, Conerly, Marcus, Lindsey et al. — Scaling monosemanticity | Sparse autoencoders of about 1M, 4M and 34M features on the middle-layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, trained to a compute-optimal loss, explain at least 65% of its variance and yield features that are multilingual and multimodal, that mostly match no neuron, and that steer the model's output when clamped, including features for unsafe code, bias, sycophancy and deception. Whether a concept has its own feature depends on its training frequency relative to the number of live features. The interpretability and steering evidence is shown on selected features, and the most strongly active features are mostly not those that matter to an answer. | Read |
| [NOTE-1179](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1179.md) | Airoldi, Blei, Fienberg and Xing — Mixed membership stochastic blockmodels | Each node has a Dirichlet membership vector over K blocks; for every ordered pair, each node draws one block for that interaction, and the edge is Bernoulli with the block pair's rate in B, scaled by a sparsity factor. So a node can take different roles with different partners. Variational EM with a nested schedule fits it. It recovers simulated blocks, matches 63 of 69 students to their grades, and maps yeast proteins to functions at about 87% against a 70% baseline. Its claim that B and the memberships do not compete for the data is asserted, not shown: memberships and B trade along a continuum given the graph, and the sparsity factor is exactly confounded with B's scale. | Read |
| [NOTE-1180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1180.md) | Rosen-Zvi, Chemudugunta, Griffiths, Smyth and Steyvers — Learning author-topic models from text corpora | Each word of a document is assigned to one of its observed authors uniformly, then to a topic from that author's distribution over a fixed number of topics, so the document–word matrix factors as ΦΘA with A the known authorship. A blocked collapsed Gibbs sampler fits it to NIPS, CiteSeer and 121,298 Enron emails. On NIPS it beats LDA in perplexity only while sixteen or fewer of a test document's words are seen, and a per-document fictitious author helps throughout. Topics are identified only up to permutation, by the authors' account, and about 80 of 100 aligned across two runs. Authorship is given, never inferred. | Read |
| [NOTE-1181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1181.md) v2 | Lindsey et al. — On the biology of a large language model | Case studies of Claude 3.5 Haiku through attribution graphs of a 30-million-feature cross-layer transcoder, each checked by inhibiting or injecting features in the model. On single prompts: "Dallas" reaches "Austin" through "Texas" features, beside a direct shortcut; a rhyme is chosen on the newline before a line and the line is written towards it; one addition lookup-table feature serves arithmetic, citations and tables; "can't answer" features are on by default and inhibited by known-entity features; a chain of thought can work backwards from a hinted answer; a jailbreak's target word is not represented before it is written; a goal finetuned into a model organism is represented across every Assistant context. The authors call these existence proofs and report a satisfying graph for about a quarter of prompts tried. | Read |
| [NOTE-1182](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1182.md) v3 | Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov and Carter — Zoom in, an introduction to circuits | A programme essay, not a study. It offers three deliberately speculative claims, as empirical claims about networks and as norms for studying them: features (directions in a layer's activation space, often single neurons) are the unit of a network; features joined by weights form circuits whose algorithms can be read off the weights; and analogous features and circuits form across models. The examples are qualitative and from InceptionV1, with the detailed evidence promised to later articles. Polysemantic neurons are named as the main obstacle, and a car feature spread over dog neurons is the first case it calls superposition. | Read |
| [NOTE-1183](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1183.md) | Wang, Hu, Du, Cheng, Wang and Zou — Fine-tuning mechanisms of LLMs via circuit analysis | When Pythia-1.4B is fine-tuned with LoRA on arithmetic tasks it starts out failing, EAP-IG circuits of 5% of edges found at successive checkpoints keep most of their nodes and change most of their edges (change rates 15–24% for nodes, 66–80% for edges), mostly in the middle layers; giving higher LoRA rank to the layers whose edges change most beats uniform and random rank allocation at similar size, and the union of two subtasks' circuits approximates a two-step task's circuit. The node–edge contrast carries no comparison against a null. | Read |
| [NOTE-1184](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1184.md) v2 | Doshi-Velez and Ghahramani — Correlated non-parametric latent feature models | Makes IBP features correlated by having observations choose categories and categories choose features, Z = f(CM). If f(0) = 0, a finite dataset has finitely many features. DP-IBP, IBP-IBP and noisy-or IBP-IBP models have O(log log N) expected features. A category can switch features on, never off: features are dependent by sharing a category, or in the DP-IBP by belonging to rival ones, and suppression is left as future work. Against the IBP the structured variants win on three of five datasets, lose on the UN data and split on the gene data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1185.md) | Ameisen et al. — Circuit tracing: revealing computational graphs in language models | A cross-layer transcoder (CLT) replaces a model's MLPs with sparse features, each reading one layer and writing to all later ones. On one prompt, freezing attention patterns and normalization denominators and adding back the reconstruction error makes a local replacement model that reproduces the model exactly and is linear between features, so its attribution graph decomposes each feature's pre-activation into edges. The graphs are hypotheses about the model, tested by perturbing features in it. The authors' own measurements: the replacement matches the model's top token on about half of prompts, and its perturbation responses agree with the model's for a layer or two and then diverge. | Read |
| [NOTE-1186](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1186.md) | Bayazit, Mueller and Bosselut — Crosscoding through time | Trains one sparse crosscoder jointly on the mid-layer activations of two or three pretraining checkpoints, so features share an index across them, and scores each feature's causal importance for subject–verb agreement at each checkpoint (Relative Indirect Effect). In Pythia-1B, OLMo-1B and BLOOM-1B the important features move, by the authors' annotation, from token-specific detectors to grammatical-category ones, and in BLOOM from language-specific to crosslingual ones for Latin-script languages; importance keeps shifting after accuracy plateaus. A method for describing which features emerge, persist and lose importance, not for predicting it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1187.md) | Marks, Rager, Michaud, Belinkov, Bau and Mueller — Sparse feature circuits | Circuits whose nodes are sparse-autoencoder features and autoencoder error terms, found in Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B by linear approximations to indirect effects. On subject–verb agreement, circuits of about 100 and 500 nodes carry half or more of the behaviour on held-out pairs, where neuron circuits need far more, but without the error nodes the feature circuits carry little. The annotated circuits show two pathways for agreement across a clause. A human removing gender features from a classifier's circuit (SHIFT) brings profession accuracy on balanced data near an oracle's, and the method runs without supervision on thousands of behaviours clustered from the Pile. | Read |
| [NOTE-1188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1188.md) | Wang, Hoogland, van Wingerden, Furman and Murfet — Refined local learning coefficients of attention heads | Restricts the local learning coefficient, singular learning theory's measure of how degenerate the loss is near a parameter, to one component's weights (weight-refined) or to another data distribution (data-refined), and tracks it per attention head over the training of a two-layer attention-only transformer. The heads' curves start alike and diverge, and cluster by the heads' functional types; refinement to code separates the two induction heads; refinement to a one-layer model's outputs locates layer-0 heads giving up simple n-grams as a circuit with layer-1 bracket-matching heads forms. One model, one run in the main text, three more seeds in an appendix. | Read |
| [NOTE-1189](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1189.md) | Elhage, Nanda, Olsson et al. — A mathematical framework for transformer circuits | An exact reformulation of attention-only transformers, and a reading of toy models with it. Heads are independent and additive, each a QK bilinear form that sets the attention pattern and an OV map that sets what moves; with patterns frozen, the logits are a sum of path terms (direct, one per head, one per composed pair of heads). Zero-layer models are bigram tables, one-layer models bigram and skip-trigram tables dominated by copying heads, and in a two-layer model the only substantial composition builds induction heads from a previous-token head by K-composition. MLP layers, two-thirds of a standard transformer's parameters, are left open. | Read |
| [NOTE-1190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1190.md) v2 | Kramár, Lieberum, Shah and Nanda — AtP*, attribution patching and its failure modes | Attribution patching (AtP) estimates every node's activation-patching effect at once from two forward passes and one backward pass, by a first-order Taylor expansion. On Pythia models from 410M to 12B, using it to order which nodes to verify by real patching finds the largest-effect nodes far more cheaply than unordered patching or sampling-based search. Its false negatives come from saturated attention softmaxes and from direct and indirect effects that nearly cancel; AtP* recomputes the softmax for queries and keys and averages gradients with one layer dropped at a time. A subsampling test gives an upper confidence bound on the size of any nodes it still misses. | Read |
| [NOTE-1191](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1191.md) | Bricken, Templeton, Batson, Chen, Jermyn et al. — Towards monosemanticity | Sparse autoencoders trained on the 512-neuron MLP layer of a one-layer transformer, at widths from 512 to 131,072, recover features that one blinded author and Claude both rate far more interpretable than neurons, that mostly match no neuron, whose effects on the output (which the autoencoder never saw) agree with their activations, and that recur in a second model trained from another seed. The features split into finer families as the dictionary widens, so the authors doubt there is one correct number of features. Everything is in one MLP layer of a one-layer model, and the detailed cases are chosen to be easy. | Read |
| [NOTE-1192](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1192.md) | Geiger, Wu, Potts, Icard and Goodman — Distributed alignment search (DAS) | Causal abstraction tests whether a network implements a high-level causal model by interchange interventions under an alignment of variables, which earlier work found by brute-force search over disjoint sets of neurons. DAS learns the alignment instead: an orthogonal rotation trained by gradient descent so that swapping rotated subspaces between inputs reproduces the high-level model's counterfactuals. In a feed-forward network trained on hierarchical equality and in BERT fine-tuned on monotonicity NLI it finds alignments with interchange intervention accuracy of 1.00 where the best localist ones reach 0.73 and 0.51. In BERT the entailment subspace decomposes into the two word identities; in the equality network it does not. On random networks DAS raises accuracy above chance only when the hidden layer is much wider than the input. | Read |
| [NOTE-1193](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1193.md) | Marks, Treutlein et al. — Auditing language models for hidden objectives | A model trained on documents describing 52 fictional reward-model biases, then by SFT and RL to exploit 47, exploits the 5 held-out biases more (17% to 45%) and new ones described in context more than other entities' biases; without the documents the held-out rate barely moves, and without SFT it still rises. Three of four blind auditing teams found the objective, all by finding the documents in the training data; the API-only team did not. Post hoc, semantic search matched the fastest team's SAE route, and SAE features found the objective from the Assistant token and from bias demonstrations where search failed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1194](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1194.md) | Hase, Bansal, Kim and Ghandeharioun — Does localization inform editing? | On 652 CounterFact facts GPT-J completes correctly, the paper asks whether the layer where causal tracing places a fact predicts where an edit of that fact succeeds. It does not. Regressing edit success on the edit layer explains most of its variance (94.7% for ROME's rewrite score), and adding the per-fact tracing effect adds at most 3.2 points, across four editing methods and five editing problems; for ROME at layer 6 the correlation is slightly negative. ROME rewrites at over 96% at every layer but the last. The authors conclude that tracing and editing answer different questions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1195](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1195.md) | Chan, Garriga-Alonso, Goldowsky-Dill, Greenblatt, Lin et al. — Causal scrubbing: results on a paren balance checker | Causal scrubbing applied to a small transformer that classifies parenthesis strings as balanced. Saying which three heads carry which test recovers 88–93% of the loss; adding how the heads compute their tests brings the combined hypothesis to 72%, the excess losses of its two halves roughly adding. Splitting one head's input into separately resampled terms raised the score from 77% to 81–84%, which the authors say is an artefact of resampling, not a better explanation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1196](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1196.md) | Chan, Garriga-Alonso, Goldowsky-Dill, Greenblatt, Lin et al. — Causal scrubbing: results on induction heads | In a two-layer attention-only model, heads 1.5 and 1.6 contribute 0.053 nats of loss on tokens where induction helps. The textbook induction circuit accounts for 35% of that. Matching on the last three tokens, layer 0's average effect, and three layer-0 heads that attend to copies of the current token raise it to 86% (91% unscrubbed, 89% with a crude rule for the previous-token head's deviations). The heads use more paths than the story names, but few positions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1197](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1197.md) | Meng, Sen Sharma, Andonian, Belinkov and Bau — Mass-editing memory in a transformer | MEMIT inserts thousands of facts into GPT-J and GPT-NeoX at once. It treats the MLP output matrix of each layer in a range that causal tracing implicates as a linear associative memory, computes for each fact a target change of the hidden state at the top of that range, and spreads it over the layers with a closed-form least-squares update for the whole batch. At 10,000 CounterFact edits on GPT-J it scores 85.8 against 50.3 for ROME applied one at a time; ROME is better at a handful of edits. | Read |
| [NOTE-1198](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1198.md) v2 | Cammarata et al. — Curve detectors | The ten curve units of InceptionV1's mixed3b are argued to detect curves: feature visualizations are curves, unit 3b:379 fires on about 11% of dataset positions and its activation level separates blind hand labels of over 800 images, curves and imperfect curves make up 55% of its contribution to expected value, synthetic curves drive it up to 24 standard deviations, and rotated dataset examples show the ten units tiling all orientations. Causality, generality and the family are argued from these; purity is argued but its mechanistic support is deferred to the next article, and no count of how much of the layer is understood is given. | Read |
| [NOTE-1199](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1199.md) v2 | Van Gael, Teh and Ghahramani — The infinite factorial hidden Markov model | Introduces the Markov Indian buffet process: each feature is a two-state Markov chain over time steps, starting off, with its own probability of switching on, a_m ~ Beta(α/M, 1), and of staying on, b_m ~ Beta(γ, δ), drawn independently. In the limit the number of features ever on is Poisson(αH_T). Used as the prior of an infinite factorial HMM, it recovers who is speaking when in mixed speech better than an IBP prior. The sequential buffet as printed has both of its predictive rules wrong. | Read |
| [NOTE-1200](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1200.md) | Geva, Schuster, Berant and Levy — Transformer feed-forward layers are key-value memories | A feed-forward layer f(x·Kᵀ)·V has the form of a key–value memory without the softmax: each hidden unit's input weights are a key and its output weights a value. In a 16-layer WikiText-103 language model, the training prefixes that most activate a sampled key share patterns humans recognize, shallow in layers 1–9 and semantic in 10–16; projected onto the vocabulary, upper-layer values agree with the next token of their key's top prefix in up to about 3.5% of units; and a layer's prediction is usually a composition of many memories, refined across layers through the residual stream. | Read |
| [NOTE-1201](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1201.md) v2 | Nanda — Attribution patching | Activation patching costs a forward pass per patched activation. Attribution patching replaces each patch by its first-order estimate on the corrupted run, (clean − corrupted activation) · gradient, so every patch costs two forward passes and one backward pass in total, and estimates add over sub-components. On IOI in GPT-2 Small it is said to track activation patching for heads and their queries, keys, values and patterns, and to fail for residual streams and the first MLP. The post argues it should fail where nonlinearities leave saturation, where an effect needs several features at once, and for large patches through LayerNorm, and frames all patching as specific to the prompt distribution chosen. | Read |
| [NOTE-1202](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1202.md) v2 | Chan, Garriga-Alonso, Goldowsky-Dill, Greenblatt et al. — Causal scrubbing: Appendix | The appendix the main post defers to. It defines % loss recovered against a label-shuffled baseline. It gives three reasons to prefer resampling ablation to zero or mean ablation. It proves that the algorithm's sampled inputs are the maximum-entropy distribution that keeps every interpretation node's inputs jointly as on the data, which the record re-checked. It explains superposition as monosemantic terms plus a resampled interference term, and builds a false hypothesis that scores ten times the model's own expected score. | Read |
| [NOTE-1203](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1203.md) | Ghahramani and Jordan — Factorial hidden Markov models | Defines the factorial HMM: M hidden chains of K states, a priori independent, whose one-hot states add their columns of W^(m) to set a Gaussian observation's mean. Exact inference costs O(TMK^{M+1}); Gibbs, completely factorized and structured variational E steps make EM tractable. On synthetic problems an HMM with K^M states overfits badly while the approximate factorial HMMs stay near exact training; on Bach chorales factorial HMMs with up to 1000 states predict better than the best HMM. Its footnote 3 on when the chains decouple is wrong unless the covariance is isotropic. | Read |
| [NOTE-1204](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1204.md) | Van Gael, Saatci, Teh and Ghahramani — Beam sampling for the infinite hidden Markov model | Introduces the beam sampler for the infinite HMM: a slice variable u_t ~ Uniform(0, π_{s_{t−1}s_t}) at each step cuts the infinitely many transitions out of each state to the finitely many above u_t, so whole trajectories are sampled exactly by forward filtering, backward sampling. Against the Gibbs sampler it mixes in fewer iterations on strongly correlated synthetic sequences, is less sensitive to the hyperprior, handles a non-conjugate Cauchy likelihood on well-log data, and costs close to O(TK) per iteration in practice; the comparisons are charts and visual judgements. | Read |
| [NOTE-1205](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1205.md) | Scherlis et al. — Polysemanticity and capacity in neural networks | In a model computing Σ(W_i·x)² + b to fit Σ v_i x_i², with independent unit-variance inputs of fourth moment k, the expected loss is (k − 1)Σ(n_i − v_i)² − 2Σn_i² + 2Σn_i²/C_i, so the marginal value of capacity is −2n_i²/C_i² and the optimum has a closed form: dense inputs (k ≤ 3) give every feature all or nothing, sparse ones (k > 3) share features whose importance lies between 2λ/(k − 1) and λ. Efficient embeddings are exactly block-semiorthogonal. Re-derived and checked. The bearing on trained networks is argued, not shown. | Read |
| [NOTE-1206](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1206.md) | Olah et al. — An overview of early vision in InceptionV1 | Every one of the 1,056 units of InceptionV1's first five layers is put in exactly one of 77 named groups, with each group's share of its layer; the shares are consistent with the unit counts. By the authors' own captions, 391 units (37%) are in groups called catch-all, broad and not well defined, low-confidence, unstudied or not understood, from 7% of conv2d2 to 48% of conv2d1. The groups are sorted by eye, and most units had "a few minutes of cursory investigation", so the census is a denominator for [THEORY-1013](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1013.md), not the criterion its promote_when asks for. | Read |
| [NOTE-1207](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1207.md) | Cammarata et al. — Curve circuits | The ten curve units of InceptionV1's mixed3b are traced back through four layers of families (Gabors, lines, early curves), each tiled along the curve's tangent with rotational and scale equivariance; negative weights from opposite early curves remove the 180° echo, which circuit editing restores. A hand-written network built from the description approximates the units on synthetic curves, by figure, and substituting it recovers 26 of the 46 top-5 classifications lost by deleting the units, on 2,000 images. The three arguments Curve Detectors deferred are supplied, mostly qualitatively. | Read |
| [NOTE-1208](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1208.md) | Griffiths and Ghahramani — Infinite latent feature models and the Indian buffet process | Introduces the Indian buffet process: the finite beta–Bernoulli feature model with π_k ~ Beta(α/K, 1) has a limit as K → ∞ on left-ordered equivalence classes, eq. (4), and a sequential buffet produces the same distribution, so objects are exchangeable and K+ ~ Poisson(αH_N). Used as the prior of an infinite binary linear-Gaussian model, its Gibbs sampler settles on about seven features for 100 photographs of four objects. The paper is the original of the authors' 2011 review. | Read |
| [NOTE-1209](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1209.md) | Knowles and Ghahramani — Infinite sparse factor analysis and infinite independent components analysis | Defines infinite sparse factor analysis and infinite ICA: Y = G(Z ⊙ X) + E, an IBP mask Z over unboundedly many sources, Gaussian or Laplacian sources, and four variants with the one- or two-parameter IBP. Its Gibbs sampler integrates a source's value out when deciding whether it is active. On 30 sparse synthetic data sets the IBP variants beat FastICA in Amari error; on ovarian cancer microarray data it finds a tissue-specific signature also found by ICA. Results are figures only, and the text misstates the IBP's total number of features. | Read |
| [NOTE-1210](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1210.md) | Teh, Görür and Ghahramani — Stick-breaking construction for the Indian buffet process | Derives the IBP's stick-breaking construction: in decreasing order the feature probabilities are μ_(k) = ∏_{l≤k} ν_l, ν_l ~ Beta(α, 1), so E[μ_(k)] = (α/(α + 1))^k, and the discarded pieces are the Dirichlet process's sticks. Slice samplers built on it, one ordered and one semi-ordered, need no conjugacy; on 120 synthetic datasets the semi-ordered one mixes as fast as Gibbs. The truncation [CASE-165](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-165.md) quotes, 8.97 features at K = 16, N = 12, α = 3, is exact here at 8.974. | Read |
| [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md) | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale — The evolution of dependence and cohesion in incipient endosymbioses | An adaptive-dynamics model in which hosts, symbionts and host–symbiont collectives are three populations. Each partner has an "obligacy" (investment in collective rather than free-living growth) and an "adhesion" (investment in synchronized, collective reproduction). The faster-growing partner, the symbiont, becomes fully obligate first. What the host's obligacy then does depends on within-collective births and deaths: it stays, rises to full dependence, or falls to none. Obligacy rises only if the collective's carrying capacity is high enough; collective growth rate does not matter. Early on, dependence evolves ahead of cohesion. That last result holds for the trait mapping the authors chose, and their own Table S1 reverses it under the opposite mapping. The authors say the available data can neither confirm nor refute it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md) | Morris, Lenski & Zinser — The Black Queen Hypothesis | Proposes that in free-living microbes, losing a costly function whose product leaks to neighbours is favoured by ordinary individual selection, and the loss runs until the remaining producers ("helpers") just supply the community, leaving most cells ("beneficiaries") dependent on a rare few. No relatedness, cooperation or collective is needed, only leakiness and frequency dependence. The one worked case is the loss of catalase-peroxidase (katG) in Prochlorococcus, which cannot survive the hydrogen peroxide that its community removes. The other cases are suggestions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1213](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1213.md) | McCutcheon, Garber, Spencer & Warren — How do bacterial endosymbionts work with so few genes? | An essay on the endosymbionts with genomes under about 200 kb, which the authors call "tipping-point endosymbionts". Below about 400 kb, symbionts almost always lose the genes to build their own envelope and to move proteins across it. Below about 200 kb, even translation erodes: ribosomal proteins, tRNAs and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases go. Their proteomes are among the most compositionally biased in bacteria. The paper asks four questions it cannot answer: where their membranes, transporters, missing translation parts and protein stability come from. Its best guess is from the host, as in organelles. The thresholds come from a hand-picked set of genomes, and the composition analysis is called preliminary. | Read |
| [NOTE-1214](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1214.md) | Di Biagio & Rovelli — Relative information, relative facts | A reformulation of relational quantum mechanics in Shannon terms. The information about A relative to B is the expected conditional information, I_{A\|B} = I_A + I_{A:B}. A is a fact relative to B when that is maximal. Only commuting variables have a joint distribution, so perspectives belong to commutative subalgebras ("classical subsystems") and not to quantum systems: a qubit has none. "Every fact is a relative fact", and the joint distribution is itself relative to a further system, generally "us". As a side result, in a von Neumann measurement the pointer's information about the measured variable grows continuously, sin²(ωt)H_A in the model. The jump is only a threshold on what counts as a fact. Merging of perspectives, Wigner's friend and the extended scenario are treated by worked examples, not theorems. | Read |
| [NOTE-1215](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1215.md) | Ashwin, Wieczorek, Vitolo & Cox — Tipping points in open systems | A classification and a criterion, not an empirical study. Tipping in an open system ẋ = f(x, λ(t)) is split into B-tipping (a bifurcation of the quasi-static attractor), N-tipping (noise carries the system out of its neighbourhood) and R-tipping, where "the system fails to track a continuously changing quasi-static attractor". In a linear model with a fixed stable M and a tipping radius R, the attractor never changes stability, yet steady drift r tips the system when ‖M‖⁻¹\|r\| > R and cannot when ‖M⁻¹‖\|r\| < R. Three examples, one with a unique globally stable equilibrium, and a global energy balance model show each type alone. Neither N- nor R-tipping needs any change of stability, so there is no reason to expect critical-slowing warnings for them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1216](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1216.md) | Flack — Coarse-graining as a downward causation mechanism | A conceptual paper, not a report of new data. Downward causation is made operational as components tuning their behaviour to their own estimates of coarse-grained variables that they collectively compute. In its weak, "apparent" form only one component need tune, to a variable slower than the behaviour producing it, and estimates need be neither correct nor shared. The strong, "effective" form needs the variable to be predictive (slow), robust, used nearly universally, agreed on, and gaining mutual information with the microscopic behaviour; only then does Flack speak of a new organizational level. Regeneration of the variable by its use is not among the criteria; what reinforces itself is convergence of the estimates. The macaque power distribution is the worked example, reviewed from earlier papers. | Read |
| [NOTE-1217](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1217.md) | Stewart, Golubitsky & Pivato — Symmetry groupoids and patterns of synchrony | In a coupled cell network, an equivalence relation on the cells gives a synchrony subspace invariant under every vector field the network admits if and only if it is balanced: every two equivalent cells have an input isomorphism that maps each input to an equivalent one (Theorem 6.5). Symmetry is one source of balance, not the only one, so robust synchrony occurs in networks with no symmetry. The dynamics on such a subspace are admissible for a smaller quotient network (Theorem 9.2), which can have a symmetry the original lacks. The paper treats existence only, not stability, and says so. | Read |
| [NOTE-1218](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1218.md) | Torres-Hugas et al. — Cycle holonomy and remote synchronization | For a phase model whose edges carry antisymmetric phase lags, the twisted Laplacian Lα = δα*δα has a zero mode exactly when every cycle holonomy is 0 mod 2π, and otherwise its smallest eigenvalue measures the residual incompatibility; for an isolated ℓ-cycle that eigenvalue is largest at holonomy π. The symmetric Sakaguchi–Kuramoto model is a different model, but on cactus graphs its lag gives each ℓ-cycle a path mismatch (ℓ − 2)α, which an associated connection is built to carry as holonomy. In the triangle–pentagon remote-synchronization motif, the pentagon's mismatch reaches π at α = π/3, where the locked branch is exactly a two-group state; but the branch has already lost transverse stability at αc ≈ 1.0164, so the holonomy marks geometry, not stability. | Read |
| [NOTE-1219](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1219.md) | Deutsch & Marletto — Constructor theory of information | A programme paper, not a theorem paper. It defines information without distinguishability: a set of attributes is an information variable when every permutation of it and its cloning are possible tasks, and distinguishability is then defined from that, which removes the circularity of (1.1). It conjectures principles III–IX for classical information, and shows informally that one extra prohibition, a union of two disjoint information observables that is not one, yields indistinguishable states, no-cloning, complementarity, deterministic unpredictability, irreducible measurement disturbance and locally inaccessible information. It calls instantiating information "an exact, intrinsic property of the substrate", so it supplies a modal, not a relational, account of what an information medium is. | Read |
| [NOTE-1220](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1220.md) | Faye & Jaksland — Barad, Bohr, and quantum mechanics | Barad's reading of Bohr is not Bohr's. For Bohr a phenomenon is the observed effect under a given experimental arrangement, epistemic and derivative, with atomic object and instrument presupposed real; Bohr was an entity realist, his relational holism epistemic, and the subject–object, knower–known and word–world dualisms are presupposed by his account, not dissolved. Nor does quantum mechanics entail agential realism: Bohmian mechanics reproduces its predictions with an ontology of individual particles, and Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics, though close, keeps systems prior to their interactions. And because Barad denies that measurement disentangles apparatus and object, she cannot borrow Rovelli's answer to the measurement problem, so even agential realism's consistency with quantum mechanics is unshown. Its merits as social theory, "if any", do not stem from quantum mechanics. | Read |
| [NOTE-1221](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1221.md) | Robinson — Sheaves are the canonical data structure for sensor integration | An expository paper. It posits six axioms for an integrated sensor system and defines a sheaf as whatever satisfies them, so "canonical" is argued by that axiomatization, not proved; the paper itself calls sheaves one of "many co-universal information representations". Its tools need less than a sheaf: on a presheaf of pseudometric spaces, the consistency radius of an assignment (the largest disagreement between an observation and the restriction of another) bounds its distance to every global section below by ε/(1 + K) when the restrictions are K-Lipschitz, and data fusion is the search for the nearest global section. In one simulated search-and-rescue scenario fusion cut the crash-location error 2–8×, and the per-restriction discrepancies singled out a biased sensor by inspection. Cohomology, for linear sheaves, flags configurations that can be locally but not globally consistent. | Read |
| [NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md) | Hansen & Ghrist — Opinion dynamics on discourse sheaves | A discourse sheaf gives each agent a private opinion space and each edge a discourse space, with a linear expression map from each agent into each of its edges. Opinion diffusion by the sheaf Laplacian converges to the projection onto the global sections: agreement in what neighbours express, not in what they hold. Letting the expression maps diffuse instead converges to the nearest sheaf in which the fixed opinions agree in expression, which the authors call "learning to lie". Nothing in the dynamics checks expression against what is held, so the agreement reached is coherence, not accuracy. | Read |
| [NOTE-1223](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1223.md) | Baez & Fong — A compositional framework for passive linear networks | Open passive linear circuits (resistors, inductors and capacitors, the latter two through the Laplace transform over the field R(s)) are the morphisms of a hypergraph category Circ of decorated cospans, and black-boxing, which keeps only the Lagrangian relation a circuit imposes between its terminals' potentials and currents, is a hypergraph functor Circ → LagRel (Thm 1.1, Thm 7.7). The relation is the graph of the differential of the power functional, the Dirichlet form left when the interior nodes are eliminated by the principle of minimum power; series resistors are the worked example. Dirichlet forms alone compose by that elimination but have no identities, so the target is Lagrangian relations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1224](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1224.md) | Singer — Angular synchronization | Angles θ₁, …, θₙ are estimated, up to one global phase, from noisy offsets θᵢ − θⱼ of which an unknown fraction are pure outliers, by the top eigenvector of the Hermitian matrix Hᵢⱼ = e^{iδᵢⱼ} or by an SDP like Goemans–Williamson's. On the complete graph a random-matrix argument puts the eigenvector's threshold at p > 1/√n good offsets, with the expected squared correlation near 1/(1 + 1/(np²)). Fano's inequality shows no algorithm can do much better: the information bound is of order √(n/m), and the polynomial method's threshold is within a factor √((L − 1)/(2 log₂ L)) of it, where 2π/L is the angular resolution, while exhaustive maximum likelihood costs O(mLⁿ). | Read |
| [NOTE-1225](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1225.md) | Spivak — Compositional dynamics in learning and mechanics | A category-theoretic syntax, the operad ArrSm of "smooth adaptive arrangements" (a responsive parameter space, a lens of output and input maps between manifolds, and a real potential), with two functorial semantics into polynomial coalgebras, i.e. discrete-time input-output machines. They differ only in the integrator: Φconf stores position and takes a descent step, Φphase stores position and momentum and takes a symplectic-Euler step. Φconf turns a parameterized map plus a loss into gradient descent with backpropagation, and a closed system with inverse-Hessian response into Newton's method. One arrangement of harmonic particles on a finite directed graph gives the discrete wave equation under Φphase and the discrete heat equation under Φconf, both governed by the symmetrized graph Laplacian. The main technical result is lens internalization, a lax symmetric monoidal functor Lens_C → C. | Read |
| [NOTE-1226](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1226.md) | Di Biagio & Rovelli — Stable facts, relative facts | A fact happens at every interaction and is relative to the system it affects. A fact relative to F is stable for another system W when W may use it as a conditional in the classical total-probability rule, eq. (3); interference is the failure of that rule. Decoherence gives stability: if F is entangled with an environment E whose branch states overlap by at most ε and W does not interact with E, eq. (3) holds for W up to O(ε). So stability is approximate (exact only as ε → 0) and relational (another system coupled differently to F–E may see interference), and a fact can be stable for W without being a fact relative to W. The authors base the ontology on relative facts, not stable ones, and read the Frauchiger–Renner contradiction and the Local Friendliness violation as the classical rule used across contexts where facts are not stable. | Read |
| [NOTE-1227](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1227.md) | Rovelli — Relational quantum mechanics | Rovelli proposes that the incorrect notion behind the measurement problem is the observer-independent state of a system, as absolute simultaneity was behind the unease with the Lorentz transformations. Two descriptions of one measurement, by the measuring system O and by an external P who treats S+O unitarily, are both correct, so "q = 1" is elliptic for "q = 1 relative to O", any physical system can be the observer, and the theory, taken as complete, is about the information (correlation) systems have about one another. The relation between two observers' views is itself a quantum fact relative to a third, so no view can be deduced from another and there is no description in toto. Values are relational; systems are not: the world is assumed decomposed into systems, each characterized by its set of yes/no questions W(S) and an information capacity N. Two information postulates give an orthomodular lattice, and a third (superposition) postulate is needed for the Hilbert-space formalism; the reconstruction is, in the author's words, "not fully successful". | Read |
| [NOTE-1228](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1228.md) | Toner & Tu — How birds fly together | A continuum theory of a flock: a coarse-grained velocity field with a convective term, a preferred speed and noise, coupled to a conserved density. Its linearized theory loses order in d ≤ 2, as the equilibrium XY model does, but the convective nonlinearity is relevant below d = 4, and in d = 2 symmetry fixes the exponents at z = 6/5, ζ = 3/5, χ = −1/5. Since χ < 0 the transverse velocity fluctuations stay bounded as the flock grows, so a flock has true long-range orientational order in two dimensions. The exactness rests on a cubic vertex staying irrelevant, which the authors "strongly suspect"; a fallback argument gives χ < 0 from z < 2, which they "expect on physical grounds". | Read |
| [NOTE-1229](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1229.md) | Zurek — Quantum Darwinism | A review. Decoherence singles out pointer states; quantum Darwinism adds that the environment is the channel observers read, and that decoherence leaves many copies of the pointer observable in it: the mutual information I(S : F_f) between the system and a fraction f of the environment rises steeply to a plateau at H_S, so R_δ = 1/f_δ fragments each hold nearly all of it, and redundancy is high only for the pointer observable. Zurek reads redundancy as objectivity. A clean unitarity argument (eq. 5) shows that only orthogonal states can be repeatably copied, without the Born rule, which he derives separately from envariance. The paper claims the measurement problem "largely settled"; it does not state the later caveat that mutual information alone does not guarantee independently accessible records. | Read |
| [NOTE-1230](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1230.md) | Jaksland — Naturalized, fundamental, and feminist metaphysics all at once | A methodological paper, not an assessment of agential realism as quantum mechanics, which it assumes. Barad holds agential realism to be naturalized metaphysics, justified by quantum mechanics and applied once, to the one reality, whose scope then extends to the lifeworld; she rejects reading it as analogy or as a template that other domains instantiate. That extension is threatened by Newtonian mechanics being a good approximation in the macroscopic domain. It survives only if some ontological features (the subject–object and word–world dualisms, representationalism) are all-or-nothing and admit no metaphysical approximation. Jaksland leaves open whether any do, finds individualism "immediately more agreeable" as something that can obtain by approximation, and argues that even without such features the independence of social theorizing from fundamental metaphysics is contingent (on the size of Planck's constant), not principled. | Read |
| [NOTE-1231](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1231.md) | Clarke, Grumberg, Jha, Lu & Veith — Counterexample-guided abstraction refinement | A model checker runs on an existential abstraction that merges concrete states, so a property true of the abstraction is true of the program (Theorem 1). An abstract counterexample is checked against the concrete system by image computation; if it has no concrete counterpart, the first abstract state where it breaks is split to separate the concrete states reachable along it from those with the transition onward, and checking runs again. The coarsest such split is stated to be NP-hard (proof omitted), so a polynomial, non-optimal split is used. For finite-state programs and ACTL* properties whose counterexamples are paths or loops, the loop ends in a real counterexample or a proof. The property is fixed throughout. | Read |
| [NOTE-1232](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1232.md) | Simon — ill structured problems | Simon argues that there is no real boundary between well and ill structured problems. Well-structuredness is judged by six conditions read as practicable, not in-principle, computability, so it is a relation between a problem and a bounded solver. On that reading even theorem proving and chess fail some conditions, chess is "well structured in the small" and ill structured "in the large", and "there are no WSPs, only ISPs that have been formalized for problem solvers" (p. 186). House design, a battleship's design by an organization and a robot in a real environment are handled by alternating a solver working on a locally well structured problem with a recognition and retrieval system that keeps modifying the problem space. Simon's conclusion is deflationary: ill structured problems may differ from well structured ones only in the size of the knowledge base, and need no qualitatively new mechanisms. | Read |
| [NOTE-1233](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1233.md) | Hansen & Ghrist — Toward a spectral theory of cellular sheaves | An exploratory programme, not a single result: the Hodge Laplacian of a weighted cellular sheaf, whose kernel in degree k is the cohomology H^k (in degree 0, the global sections), with sheaf versions of spectral graph theory's basics: harmonic extension, an eigenvalue bound for normalized sheaves, interlacing, pushforward and covering spectra, product spectra, effective resistance and a sparsification theorem. The heat flow ẋ = −Δ^k x converges exponentially to the orthogonal projection onto the harmonic cochains (Prop. 8.1). Kron reduction fails for general sheaves, because an interior vertex can impose constraints on the boundary that no pairwise sheaf expresses. A Cheeger inequality is not proved; the applications in §8 are sketches. | Read |
| [NOTE-1234](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1234.md) | Kay et al. — Dated gene duplications and the assembly of eukaryotes | A relaxed molecular clock dates 135 gene duplications that happened on the two stem lineages of eukaryotes, inside a species tree dated with 18 fossil calibrations. The authors take the onset of duplications in genes of alphaproteobacterial origin, about 2.2 billion years ago, as the mark of mitochondrial endosymbiosis. Most duplications of archaeal origin are older than that, including ones in actin, tubulin, vesicle trafficking and nuclear-targeted families, so the host was already elaborating its cytoskeleton, endomembranes and nuclear machinery. Most duplications of non-alphaproteobacterial bacterial genes come later, which the authors take as evidence against serial endosymbiosis. Each duplication date is a maximum age for its paralogues' functions, many intervals reach below 2.2 billion years, and the order of phagocytosis and the mitochondrion is left open by the authors. | Read |
| [NOTE-1235](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1235.md) | Campbell et al. — Changes in endosymbiont complexity drive host-level compensatory adaptations in cicadas | In cicadas whose endosymbiont Hodgkinia has split into many lineages, each essential, the mother must put every lineage into every egg. A simulation shows that random transmission would need far more cells as lineages multiply and grow uneven. Counts in eggs of four species find Sulcia numbers roughly constant, and Hodgkinia numbers up to about six times higher in Magicicada septendecim than in a single-lineage species. Amplicon sequencing found every tracked Hodgkinia genotype in every egg sampled. The transmission route looks the same under the light microscope. Only M. septendecim differs significantly; the six-lineage species does not. So the compensation rests on one species. The authors call the raised titre a cost of fragmentation, and speculate that it could feed further splitting. | Read |
| [NOTE-1236](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1236.md) | Shigenobu, Watanabe, Hattori, Sakaki & Ishikawa — Genome sequence of the endocellular bacterial symbiont of aphids Buchnera sp. APS | The first complete genome of an obligate insect endosymbiont. Buchnera APS, from the pea aphid, has a 640,681-bp chromosome with 583 ORFs and two small plasmids. It is a subset of the E. coli gene set, produced by loss from a larger common ancestor. It keeps the pathways for the amino acids its host cannot make, lacks almost all of those the host can, and draws some precursors from the host, so the two partners' pathways interlock. It also lacks phospholipid and lipopolysaccharide synthesis, almost all transcriptional regulators, and recA and uvrABC. The authors infer that it can live only in the bacteriocyte and compare it to an organelle. Everything here is read from gene content; no experiment on the symbiont is reported, and the host's dependence is asserted from the literature, not shown. | Read |
| [NOTE-1237](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1237.md) | Bernabeu, Manzano-Morales, Marcet-Houben & Gabaldón — Gene ancestries reveal diverse microbial associations during eukaryogenesis | A fresh reconstruction of the last eukaryotic common ancestor's proteome from three 100-genome eukaryotic datasets, with each family's origin read from its sister group in a maximum-likelihood tree. Under thresholds tuned to maximize assignments to Alphaproteobacteria and Asgard archaea, two further bacterial donors pass in every dataset, Myxococcota (3.92% of the proteome) and Planctomycetota (2.24%), comparable to Alphaproteobacteria (3.99%) and Asgard (3.28%). A control that removes Alphaproteobacteria from the database does not reproduce their pattern. About 4.5% of families have a viral sister, mostly giant viruses. Stem-length distributions place Asgard earliest and Planctomycetota before the mitochondrion and Myxococcota. The authors read this as waves of transfer from several partners and challenge two-partner models. They concede their data say nothing about whether any donor was a symbiont. | Read |
| [NOTE-1238](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1238.md) | Imachi et al. — Isolation of an Asgard archaeon at the prokaryote–eukaryote interface | After 12 years from sampling to culture, an archaeon of the Asgard group, Ca. Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum MK-D1, was obtained in stable co-culture with a methanogen (not alone, hence the Candidatus name). It is a small coccus, about 550 nm across, doubling in 14–25 days. It degrades amino acids only in syntrophy, handing off hydrogen and formate to partners that can be swapped. It has long, often branching membrane protrusions and no visible internal compartments. It is the closest cultured relative of eukaryotes, among cultured organisms only. From its genome and other Asgard genomes the authors propose that the Asgard ancestor was a partner-dependent amino-acid degrader. The entangle–engulf–endogenize model they build on it is a hypothesis that the authors call not definitive. | Read |
| [NOTE-1239](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1239.md) | Santana-Molina, Williams, Snel & Spang — Chimeric origins and dynamic evolution of central carbon metabolism in eukaryotes | Sixty-four gene-family phylogenies for eukaryotic central carbon metabolism (glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, pyruvate and acetate conversion, and the TCA cycle), set against a 317-marker eukaryotic species tree. LECA had essentially the whole pathway set. Its enzymes came from several sources: six putative Asgard contributions, mostly cytosolic glycolytic and pentose-phosphate enzymes (support between 39% and 97%, two cases ambiguous); seventeen alphaproteobacterial ones, mostly mitochondrial and ten of them in the TCA cycle; and others from various bacteria, with no third dominant donor. Since then, loss, horizontal replacement and retargeting have reshaped the pathways, and targeting no longer follows origin. The authors read the split, archaeal glycolysis in the cytosol and bacterial TCA in the mitochondrion, as support for syntrophy models. The split is what any archaeal-host, bacterial-endosymbiont model predicts, so it does not single syntrophy out. | Read |
| [NOTE-1240](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1240.md) | Pittis & Gabaldón — Late acquisition of mitochondria by a chimaeric host | For 1,078 eukaryotic protein families inferred to be present in LECA, the length of the branch joining each family to its closest prokaryotic relatives, divided by the family's median branch length within eukaryotes, is shortest for families of alphaproteobacterial origin and mitochondrial location, longer for other bacterial families (endomembrane-associated), and longest for archaeal families (nucleus and information processing). Read as time, that puts the mitochondrion last, into a host whose proteome was already chimaeric. The reading of length as time needs rates before and after LECA to be proportional, the alphaproteobacterial difference from other bacteria is marginal (P = 0.044), and stem length also falls when a closer relative is sampled, as the paper's own Lokiarchaeota control shows. | Read |
| [NOTE-1241](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1241.md) | Sørensen, Stiller, Kröninger & Nowack — Protein import into bacterial endosymbionts and evolving organelles | A review of the evidence that hosts import their own proteins into bacterial endosymbionts, which has long been taken to mark an organelle off from an endosymbiont. Import of hundreds of nucleus-encoded proteins is established, by proteomics of isolated endosymbionts, in two systems only: the chromatophore of Paulinella and the nitroplast of Braarudosphaera. In both, the imported proteins come mostly from the host's own genes and from bacteria other than the endosymbiont, and the authors say that gene transfer from the endosymbiont "is not a precondition" for genetic integration. Elsewhere, in a trypanosomatid, a diatom and four insects, there are one to seven imported or targeted proteins per system, each found by antibodies or proteomics. The authors propose an order, effector proteins first and dependence on an imported redundant protein second, which they call plausible on limited data. The import mechanisms are almost entirely unknown. | Read |
| [NOTE-1242](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1242.md) | Tobiasson, Luo, Wolf & Koonin — Dominant contribution of Asgard archaea to eukaryogenesis | A large phylogenomic survey that assigns each widespread eukaryotic protein family to its most likely prokaryotic sister by likelihood weights on constrained trees. In the 4,290 best-resolved families, Asgard archaea take about half of all likelihood weight and lead in nearly every functional system, information processing above all. Alphaproteobacteria contribute a small, coherent set centred on the mitochondrion (oxidative phosphorylation, Fe–S cluster assembly, mitochondrial translation). About a third of families point to other bacteria, scattered across functions with no pathway from one donor except a narrow Myxococcota signal, which the authors read as piecemeal gene transfer and not further symbioses. A stem-length analysis leads them to doubt that stem lengths time gene acquisition. They favour a complex Asgard ancestor that took up the mitochondrion late. The limiting caveat, theirs, is sparse and biased genome sampling. | Read |
| [NOTE-1243](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1243.md) | Karnkowska et al. — The oxymonad genome displays canonical eukaryotic complexity without a mitochondrion | An inventory of the draft genome of Monocercomonoides exilis, an oxymonad gut commensal and the only well-studied eukaryote with no mitochondrion. Apart from the mitochondrion, peroxisomes and the machinery for degrading them, nothing in the cell looks reduced: about 75 Mb, 16,768 genes, 31,693 introns, and canonical systems for DNA replication and repair, transcription, the cytoskeleton, membrane trafficking and autophagy. It has kept more ancestral eukaryotic protein families than the parasitic metamonads. The only changes the authors tie to the loss are two preadaptations, the SUF system for Fe–S clusters, which all examined relatives share, and the loss of the glycine cleavage system and SHMT, plus the loss of mitophagy. No gene was found that compensates for the absence. The work is homology searches on a draft genome, with two cells imaged by FIB-SEM. | Read |
| [NOTE-1244](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1244.md) | Supporters, Followers, Fans, and Flaneurs: A Taxonomy of Spectator Identities in Football | A conceptual taxonomy of how spectators identify with football clubs, on two axes: traditional–consumer (the basis of investment) and hot–cool (how central the club is to the self). Supporters are traditional and hot; followers traditional and cool; fans consumer and hot; flâneurs consumer and cool. Giulianotti argues that football's "hypercommodification" since the late 1980s moves identification from the supporter towards the flâneur, while clubs still depend on supporters to make the spectacle flâneurs consume. Ideal types, with no data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1245](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1245.md) | Preregistered Replication and Extension of "Moral Hypocrisy: Social Groups and the Flexibility of Virtue" | Two preregistered online experiments (Prolific, US). One used minimal groups (n = 590 analysed) and one used Democrats versus Republicans (n = 577). Neither replicated Valdesolo and DeSteno's intergroup moral hypocrisy (the original N was 76 and d was 1.11); the minimal-group contrast is statistically equivalent to zero. In minimal groups, in-group favouritism appeared only as it rose with collective identification (interaction b = −.39); the in-group/out-group contrast was not significant (p = .07). Partisans judged an out-party member's identical selfish act as less fair (p = .003). About a third of those free to choose took no advantage for themselves. | Read |
| [NOTE-1246](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1246.md) | Cultural Trauma: Slavery and the Formation of African American Identity | The book's first chapter, read alone. Cultural trauma is a loss of identity and meaning in a group, not an individual wound, and need not be felt by everyone in it. Slavery became the trauma of African Americans "in retrospect": in the 1880s, when Reconstruction failed and white North and South reconciled around a memory of slavery as benign, a generation never enslaved made its memory the "primal scene" of a collective identity.
