Membership was set by "a common fate, not necessarily a common experience", whether or not one's ancestors were enslaved. Intellectuals and social movements carry the trauma; each social generation reworks it; it became national memory only with the civil rights movement. The chapter is a framework and a plan; the evidence is in chapters 2–6. | Read |
| [NOTE-1247](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1247.md) | The epistemic challenge to longtermism | A model of the epistemic objection to longtermism. A $1 million existential-risk intervention changes the chance that civilization exists in 1000 years by a conservative 2 x 10^-14, and its effect lasts until an "exogenous nullifying event" arrives at a constant rate r, which acts as an exponential discount. Against a global-health benchmark of 10,000 QALYs, it wins if r is below about 0.000135 per year with interstellar settlement, or 0.000000012 per year on Earth alone. Small credences in settlement, low r, fast travel or star-sized value make it win by orders of magnitude, but then the win can rest on probabilities as small as 10^-18. So the case for longtermism depends on non-obvious empirical claims or on Pascalian fanaticism, and its horizon may be thousands or millions of years, not billions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1248](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1248.md) | Persistent epigenetic differences associated with prenatal exposure to famine in humans | Sixty people conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 (daily rations averaging 667 kcal) had, about 58 years later, less methylation of the imprinted IGF2 gene's DMR in blood than their unexposed same-sex siblings: 0.488 vs 0.515, −5.2%, 0.48 SD, P = 5.9 × 10⁻⁵, lower in the exposed sibling in 43 of 60 pairs. Sixty-two people exposed only late in gestation were born 296 g lighter but showed no difference, and the timing interaction was significant. Birth weight did not track methylation. The authors read it as the first evidence that a transient early-gestation exposure is recorded as a lasting epigenetic change in humans. The exposure is the person's own; no later generation is studied. | Read |
| [NOTE-1249](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1249.md) | Retention of Memory through Metamorphosis: Can a Moth Remember What It Learned As a Caterpillar? | Tobacco hornworm caterpillars trained to pair ethyl acetate with mild shock avoided it as fifth instars (78%, N = 41) and, four to five weeks and a metamorphosis later, as moths (77%, N = 27); 80% of tracked individuals chose the same way at both stages. Controls showed no effect. Washing trained pupae or scenting naive ones changed nothing, so residue on the pupal case does not explain the adult aversion. Third-instar training survived two larval molts but not metamorphosis. By analogy with Drosophila the authors place the memory in late-forming mushroom-body neurons that keep their projections through pupation, a hypothesis they did not test. | Read |
| [NOTE-1250](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1250.md) | Trauma, prejudice, large-group identity and psychoanalysis | A memorial lecture at the Freud Museum. Large-group identity is a tent's canvas worn over each person's individual identity, fixed in childhood through what parents deposit and unchangeable after adolescence. In two decades of unofficial dialogues, Volkan saw participants who felt their large-group identity threatened turn, with emotion, to an injury their ancestors suffered centuries ago. The shared image of such an event, real or mythologized, changes function across generations and becomes an identity marker: a chosen trauma. It feeds entitlement to recover what was lost and, in a "time collapse", makes the old event feel recent, as with Kosovo 1389 under Milošević. The Holocaust is not a chosen trauma: it is recent, its stories are alive, and it is mourned rather than kept as a wound for revenge. | Read |
| [NOTE-1251](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1251.md) | Self-categorization and social identification: Making sense of us and them | A textbook account of the social identity perspective. Self-categorization is hierarchical (personal, social, human) and situational (salience = accessibility × fit, with comparative and normative fit), and leads to depersonalization. Social identification has seven components (Ashmore et al. 2004). Social identity theory explains minimal-group bias by positive distinctiveness. Multiple-categorization models predict when bias falls. Unlike Hornsey 2008, it says the self-esteem hypothesis "has received extensive empirical support". | Read |
| [NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md) | A Perfect Moral Storm: Climate Change, Intergenerational Ethics and the Problem of Moral Corruption | Climate change is a "perfect moral storm" in which three storms converge. The global storm is a tragedy of the commons between states. The intergenerational storm is worse: carbon dioxide stays in the air for centuries, 17–33% of it for a thousand years by the estimate quoted, so the benefits of emitting go to the present and the costs to later generations. Every generation then has reason to overpollute, and since generations do not coexist, no institution or reciprocity can stop it. The theoretical storm is that our theories cope badly with such cases. Together they make moral corruption easy: each generation can seem to take the problem seriously while exploiting its position in time, and need not admit it, "either to others, or, perhaps more importantly, to itself". | Read |
| [NOTE-1253](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1253.md) | Social Identity Theory and Self-categorization Theory: A Historical Review | A short critical history of the social identity approach. Social identity theory (Tajfel & Turner 1979) is about intergroup relations: positive distinctiveness and the socio-structural variables of status, permeability, stability and legitimacy. Self-categorization theory (Turner et al. 1987) is about categorization at levels of inclusiveness, salience by accessibility and fit, and depersonalization. It records two dead ends (identification predicting bias, and the self-esteem hypothesis) and a later softening of the "functional antagonism" between personal and social identity. Hornsey lists the criticisms and declines to answer them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1254](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1254.md) | Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance: Myths and Mechanisms | A review. In plants and C. elegans, epigenetic states pass through many generations, carried by small RNA, DNA methylation and histone H3K9 methylation, mostly at transposons and transgenes. In mammals, two rounds of reprogramming, in the germline and the early embryo, erase most marks; the few bona fide epialleles are at retrotransposons. An exposed pregnant female's effects count as transgenerational only in F3, an exposed male's only in F2. Environmentally induced changes are rarely inherited and more rarely adaptive. Human nutritional evidence is intergenerational and confounded: "so far there is little support". Human culture, the authors say with Gould, is the inheritance that is Lamarckian. | Read |
| [NOTE-1255](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1255.md) | Intergenerational transmission of paternal trauma among US Civil War ex-POWs | Children of Union Army veterans born after the Civil War and surviving to 45 (19,903 children of 6,367 fathers). Sons of men held in Confederate camps when prisoner exchanges had stopped and conditions were worst had a mortality hazard 1.11 times that of non-POWs' sons (P = 0.009); exchange-period POWs' sons and all daughters were unaffected. Within families, sons born after the war died at 2.23 times the rate of brothers born before it (P = 0.056). The effect was 1.20 among sons born in the second quarter and nil in the fourth, read as maternal nutrition reversing it. Socioeconomic and maternal controls left it unchanged. By elimination the authors favour an epigenetic route but cannot reject psychological or cultural ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-1256](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1256.md) | Identity fusion: The interplay of personal and social identities in extreme group behavior | Five preliminary studies and three two-wave experiments with Spanish students. A single pictorial item, the self as a small circle wholly inside a circle for Spain, picks out the "fused" (about 40%). Fusion is bimodal, related to but distinct from identification (r = .26 to .56) and specific to one group. The fused said they would fight and die for Spain more than others would. Activating their personal self, by challenging negative self-views or asking what they would fight for themselves, raised that willingness further; it did nothing for the nonfused. The authors read this as personal and social identity being "functionally equivalent" in the fused, against self-categorization theory's functional antagonism. | Read |
| [NOTE-1257](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1257.md) | Surviving Death, Again | Johnston withdraws Surviving Death's account of survival. There, he recalls, the resurrection hope failed and the substitute was living on "in the onward rush of humankind", on the view that we are higher-order things whose deepest future-directed attitudes fix which embodiments are ours. Now he holds that every reductionist account of personal identity breeds "fellow travelers" with moral status and conflicting interests: personites, R-variants, overlapping "Theons" and modal variants. To avoid them, he holds, we must be essentially embodied wills whose present bodies are not essential, so re-embodiment after death is possible. He argues that emergent substance dualism is a "fig leaf" for divine creation, and gives non-reductive relations of subserving, implementing and interdependence between mental and neural events. | Read |
| [NOTE-1258](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1258.md) | The stability of memories during brain remodeling: A perspective | A perspective, typed an addendum, with no new data. Learned behaviour is reported to survive brain remodelling in metamorphosing insects (odour-shock aversions in Drosophila and Manduca), regenerating planaria (McConnell's 1960s savings and the authors' 2013 place learning) and hibernating squirrels and marmots (hippocampal dendrites pruned in torpor, operant memory kept after six months). The authors argue that synaptic plasticity alone cannot explain lasting memory, posit a non-synaptic "blueprint", and propose that a planarian's memory may be stored outside the brain and imprinted on the new one, perhaps through neoblasts or bioelectric networks. The insect mechanism is called unknown; the planarian one untested. | Read |
| [NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md) | Future self-continuity: how conceptions of the future self transform intertemporal choice | A review, mostly of the author's own work. Following Parfit, people who feel less connected to their future self treat it like a stranger and save less for it. Similarity to one's self in ten years, chosen as overlapping circles adapted from Aron's scale, predicted patient choices and assets; a future self represented neurally like another person predicted steeper discounting (r = .47); seeing one's age-progressed face raised saving; respect for the elderly tracked and raised saving. Directly reported liking and caring for the future self did not predict choice, but were near ceiling. The future self may extend, at life's end, to one's offspring. | Read |
| [NOTE-1260](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1260.md) | Psychometric validation of the Loyola Generativity Scale in Chilean teachers: evidence for a three factor structure | 430 Chilean elementary teachers completed a Spanish Loyola Generativity Scale, McAdams and de St. Aubin's 20 items on a 4-point scale. Four items were dropped for poor sampling adequacy. Of one- to four-factor solutions, three factors were retained (RMSEA = 0.043, CFI = 0.989, 55.1% of variance); four fit slightly better but were judged over-extracted. Its factors: Generative Inefficacy, three negatively worded items; Generative Action, eight items; and Generative Legacy, three items on symbolic continuity. Action and Legacy correlate .45. The authors call the analysis confirmatory, but it chooses the number of factors from the data. Only 14 of the 16 retained items appear in the final solution, without comment. | Read |
| [NOTE-1261](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1261.md) | Generativity as a Route to Active Ageing | Two Heidelberg gerontologists read generativity, Erikson's "concern in establishing and guiding the next generation", as the psychological form of an ethical "joint responsibility" that lasts into very old age. They follow McAdams: generativity is driven by cultural demand and an inner desire, which is a need to be needed and a need for symbolic immortality, "to invest resources and potentials into things that outlive the self". It is not altruism, and its motives can be selfish or altruistic. In 3,308 older adults in Mexico, Spain and Germany, generativity predicted optimism and life satisfaction. An intervention of intergenerational projects in Belarus, Russia and Ukraine raised generativity scores in old and young. No statistics are given. | Read |
| [NOTE-1262](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1262.md) | Group-level self-definition and self-investment: A hierarchical (multicomponent) model of in-group identification | Seven studies with Dutch students. Identification has five components on two correlated dimensions (r = .61 to .77): self-definition (self-stereotyping, in-group homogeneity) and self-investment (solidarity, satisfaction, centrality). The model fit Dutch, European and university identification better than one-factor or cognitive-versus-affective models. Weeks to months later, the components predicted different reactions. Shown their group's mistreatment of Rwandan asylum seekers, those who saw themselves as like the average European felt more guilt, while those satisfied with being European, and for whom it was central, legitimized the policy. The self-circle overlap measure correlated with self-investment as much as with self-stereotyping. | Read |
| [NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md) | Future People, the Non-Identity Problem, and Person-Affecting Principles | Most of our choices change who will exist, so a policy that makes later lives much worse may be worse for no one who ever lives. Narrow person-affecting principles then imply that such a policy, or ending human history by having no children, is not wrong. Parfit rejects them, and retracts his own 1984 appeal to an impersonal principle. Being caused to exist with a life worth living is an intrinsic "existential benefit". On the Wide Principle an outcome is worse if it benefits people less, which solves the non-identity problem in person-affecting terms and keeps "better than" transitive. A Wide Dual Principle, counting benefits to each and benefits to all, does not imply the Repugnant Conclusion. We may favour present people in what we do, but if every generation does, "we and our successors might together wreck the Earth". | Read |
| [NOTE-1264](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1264.md) | Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance: a critical perspective | A Perspective. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance needs the environment to instruct the epigenome and the marks to reach the next generation; in mammals both are weak. Marks follow transcription factors; DNA methylation is stripped from gametes and early embryos; no validated mechanism links environment to epigenome, and organisms actively erase marks. The Agouti diet effect did not replicate, rodent effects fade or fail to replicate, and the one robust paternal effect seems not to go through sperm epigenetics. The Swedish famine study ignored cultural transmission and failed to replicate in a larger cohort; the Holocaust study had 32 people. The article does not separate inter- from transgenerational effects. | Read |
| [NOTE-1265](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1265.md) | A critical view on transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans | A Comment. In mammals, germline epigenetic inheritance must cross the Weismann barrier and two waves of reprogramming, and human studies are confounded by genetic, ecological and cultural inheritance. The Dutch Hunger Winter shows fetal programming, not germline transmission; grandparental food-supply and Prader–Willi findings await replication; familial epimutations are usually secondary to a nearby mutation. A roadmap: exclude the other inheritances (F3 after an exposed pregnant female, F2 after an exposed male), find the factor in pure germ cells, show it causes the effect. In humans only genetic effects can be excluded. Cultural transmission "very likely" outweighs any epigenetic inheritance; the author remains sceptical. | Read |
| [NOTE-1266](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1266.md) | Being one of us. Group identification, joint actions, and collective intentionality | "Group identification", as philosophers of shared agency use it (Pacherie, Petersson), runs together two separable processes. One is adopting the group's perspective, asking "what should we do?". The other is self-transformation, coming to understand oneself as a member. The first can occur without the second (the discursive dilemma) and the second without the first (toddlers' joint action before age three). Self-transformation is not a belief but a Pushmi-Pullyu representation: "you are a member of us; act as such", at once describing and motivating, triggered by cues such as joint attention, and not under direct rational control. A conceptual paper. | Read |
| [NOTE-1267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1267.md) | Population ethical intuitions | Nine experiments with US online samples. People require more happiness than suffering for a population to be better existing than not (about 75% happy; about 61% when the two are stated to be equally intense). Yet they judge adding one extremely happy person as good as adding one extremely unhappy person is bad: they reject the intuition of neutrality and the procreation asymmetry. With averages fixed they prefer larger happy and smaller unhappy populations, but the preference for more happy people fades and, at a billion against ten billion, reverses. With totals fixed they prefer higher averages. In conflicts averagism tends to win, to the point of preferring to add near-maximally unhappy people who raise the average. Prompts to reflect move judgements toward totalism. | Read |
| [NOTE-1268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1268.md) | Social Influence and Group Identity | A review of the group-identity account of social influence, grounded in self-categorization theory. Influence from a group need not be compliance for approval: when the group is a level of the self, in-group sources produce private acceptance, so influence is "partly self-influence". Classic conformity, obedience, minority-influence, emergency, helping and contagion findings are reread as bounded by shared identity. Identification, prototypicality, intergroup threat and context moderate the effect. Isolation and anonymity strengthen group influence, and crowd members switch to a group identity rather than losing the self. The evidence is reported, not presented. | Read |
| [NOTE-1269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1269.md) | Shaping Humanity's Longterm Trajectory | Humanity's value per unit time is a curve, the future's value the area under it, and an intervention's value the area between two curves. Value must be summable and separable across time, and there is no pure time preference. Four idealised changes have values independent of the curve's shape. An advancement is worth about (v_τ − v_0)δt, which does not grow with the future's duration, and is negative if the end comes sooner too. A speed-up scales with (v_τ − v̄)τ, a gain with τ, an enhancement with v̄τ. Raising near-term survival by a factor γ_p is worth (γ_p − 1)v̄τ, like an enhancement, and is more surely contingent. So advancing progress rarely rivals existential risk reduction: on a million-year future a year's advancement equals a one-in-a-million gain in survival. | Read |
| [NOTE-1270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1270.md) | The Psychology of Existential Risk: Moral Judgments about Human Extinction | Parfit's three outcomes, put to laypeople: no catastrophe, 80% of humanity killed, 100% killed. Most judge extinction bad and to be prevented (78% on a binary item), but of those who rank the outcomes as expected only 23% (UK), 19% (US) and 37% (Oxford students) judge the step from 80% to 100% the greater. More do when the victims are zebras (44%, 35%), when the catastrophe sterilizes rather than kills (47%, 29%), or when reminded that only extinction ends humanity's future (50%, 39%). A majority do only when the surviving future is described as long and utopian (77%, 67%, 77%). Existential-risk mitigators do so unprompted (86%). The authors read this as a focus on immediate harm to fellow humans and neglect of the long term. | Read |
| [NOTE-1271](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1271.md) | Managing the Terror of Publication Bias: A Systematic Review of the Mortality Salience Hypothesis | Re-runs Burke et al.'s meta-analysis of the mortality-salience hypothesis on a decade more data, with five tools for bias. Uncorrected, 635 effects give g = 0.81 (about r = .37), close to Burke et al.'s r = .35. Selection models (g = 0.36) and WAAP-WLS (g = 0.39) put the average near r = .18; PET-PEESE finds no positive effect. A p-curve of 825 focal tests finds evidential value at 25% average power; z-curve puts the expected replication rate at 19% and the expected discovery rate at 8%. Five of nine preregistered replications succeeded. True effects are so heterogeneous that 95% of them span r = −.47 to .66. The authors conclude some MS effects are real, the average is about half the published one, and most studies could not detect it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1272](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1272.md) | The Oral History of 'I'm the Juggernaut, Bitch!' | Journalism. Xavier Nazario and Randy Hayes redubbed a 1990s X-Men episode in November 2005 and posted it on 14 February 2006. Within months it had millions of views. A TV news segment, before the film's release, reported the line "making it into the new X-Men movie". The film says "I'm the Juggernaut, bitch!" Kinberg, via Polygon: "That was a reshoot Ratner line." That Ratner was "likely a fan" of the video is Siegel's inference, not testimony. The videos were later taken down amid Viacom's takedowns, and the creators were never paid. | Read |
| [NOTE-1273](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1273.md) | Leaving a Legacy: Intergenerational Allocations of Benefits and Burdens | Six experiments on intergenerational allocation. Framing a climate decision as leaving burdens rather than using up benefits raised concern with one's legacy, felt responsibility and affinity toward future generations, ethical concern and moral emotions. In allocation tasks people favoured themselves more with benefits than with burdens, but only when the other person would receive the resource in the future, and only when they themselves were a party to the trade-off. Perceived ethical considerations accounted for the first condition. The authors read this as legacy concern, the wish to extend the self beyond death. Legacy concern was measured only in the attitude studies, never alongside an allocation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1274](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1274.md) | Empirical Approaches to Altruism | A survey by Doris, Stich, Walmsley and Schulz. Under the standard account, altruism means an ultimate desire for another's well-being, and evolutionary and social-science senses of the word do not bear on it. Batson's experiments tell against the social-punishment and aversive-arousal versions of egoism. Self-other merging would make helping egoistic only if the helper took herself to be numerically identical with the other. The four measures used in the 1997 exchange test likeness or something unclear, not identity. On the causal question, the entry says only that Batson et al. corrected Cialdini's methods and found empathy's role "clearly evident". Altruism is still unproven: divine punishment, principles, norms and habit remain open explanations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1275](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1275.md) | Culture and the self: Implications for cognition, emotion, and motivation | A theoretical review. Cultures construe the self as independent, bounded and defined by inner attributes (most clearly American), or as interdependent, defined by relationships with specific others in specific contexts (Japanese and other Asian, also African, Latin American, Hindu, southern European). For the interdependent self "others are included within the boundaries of the self", without "a merging of self and other". This is predicted to shape cognition (more knowledge of others, contextual self-description), emotion (other-focused over ego-focused emotions) and motivation (achievement for others, modesty over self-enhancement). The authors name "a self defined in relationship to others" as an alternative to both selfishness and selflessness. | Read |
| [NOTE-1276](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1276.md) | Pair-Bonding as Inclusion of Other in the Self: A Literature Review | A short review by Aron's group. In a close relationship each partner experiences the other's resources, perspectives and identities as to some extent their own (Aron et al. 1991). The single-item IOS circle scale is the standard measure, validated as subjective closeness. It goes with cognitive signs of inclusion: slower "me/not-me" judgements on traits where the partner differs, more self–partner confusions in memory, plural pronouns. Recent studies tie overlap to self-like treatment of a partner. High-overlap people keep a positive view of a partner shown inferior. Their sleep suffers more from a partner's pain. Honour-endorsing men high in overlap are more aggressive toward a partner's moral violation. The review adds a two-dimensional model of relational self-change and a measure of perceived inclusion. No new data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1277](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1277.md) | Empathy, Altruism, and Group Identification | Cialdini et al. said empathy-induced helping is due to self-other merging. May argued that no reading of "merging" is both coherent and explanatory. The authors read it as group identification. In empathizing with Y, X comes to conceive of Y as part of X's social self, so Y's welfare is constitutive of X's first-person plural welfare. This explains Batson's similarity-induced helping in the same way as minimal-group favouritism, and needs no belief in being two bodies, since identification is a Pushmi-Pullyu representation (Salice and Miyazono). Such helping is altruistic at the individual level and egoistic at the group level. The empirical rebuttal by Batson et al. (1997) is set aside as out of scope. | Read |
| [NOTE-1278](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1278.md) | Social Identity Theory's Self-Esteem Hypothesis: A Review and Some Suggestions for Clarification | A qualitative review of over 40 studies of social identity theory's self-esteem hypothesis: discrimination raises self-esteem (corollary 1) and low self-esteem motivates discrimination (corollary 2). The theory implies specific social state self-esteem, esteem for this group, now; most studies measured global personal trait self-esteem. Counting experiments, corollary 1 has 18 for and 13 against, corollary 2 has 7 for and 28 against, and one of eight full tests supports both. Nine studies find high personal self-esteem goes with the most discrimination. Discrimination seems to raise self-esteem without being motivated by a need for it, so the hypothesis fails "in its full and unqualified form". The authors propose a narrower version in specific social state self-esteem. | Read |
| [NOTE-1279](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1279.md) | Activating the legacy motive mitigates intergenerational discounting in the climate game | A climate collective-risk game with 30 groups of six. When saving the group's endowments paid the players the next day, 9 of 10 groups reached the target; when it paid for trees for future generations, 2 of 10 did; with three messages added to activate the legacy motive (death awareness, the powerlessness of future generations, and paying forward a past generation's sacrifice), 7 of 10 did. Each message raised investment. The messages restored a fair-share norm rather than extra giving. No manipulation checks and no control message, so which mechanism worked is unknown. The authors call the legacy motive a way of leveraging self-interest. | Read |
| [NOTE-1280](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1280.md) | Group Identity, Social Influence, and Collective Action Online: Extensions and Applications of the SIDE Model | The SIDE model as its authors state it. Deindividuation theory's account, in which anonymity and immersion cut self-awareness and release antinormative behaviour, is rejected. Anonymity within a group makes the salient identity more salient. With a group identity salient, people conform more to its local norms. With personal identity salient, they move away from the group norm. Depersonalization is "the emergence of group in the self", not a loss of self. A strategic dimension adds that anonymity to a powerful out-group frees in-group-normative behaviour it would punish. The model is extended to visible media, online communities and collective action. The evidence is reported, not presented. | Read |
| [NOTE-1281](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1281.md) | Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations | Male mice fear-conditioned to acetophenone or propanol before mating had sons and grandsons, never exposed to either odour, who startled more to, and detected at lower concentrations, the odour their grandfather or father had learned, and not the other. Sons and grandsons of acetophenone-trained males had more olfactory neurons carrying its receptor (M71, gene Olfr151) and larger M71 glomeruli; the anatomy, not tested behaviourally, held in IVF offspring carried by surrogates. Mothers conditioned before mating gave the same results, which survived cross-fostering. Olfr151 was less methylated in F0 and F1 sperm (n = 12 vs 10; 4 vs 4), not in the olfactory epithelium. The authors call it inherited sensitivity to a salient cue, not inherited fear. | Read |
| [NOTE-1282](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1282.md) | Evolution, altruism and cognitive architecture: a critique of Sober and Wilson's argument for psychological altruism | Sober and Wilson argue, from parental care, that natural selection would favour an ultimate desire for the child's welfare over hedonism, on grounds of reliability. Stich grants that evolutionary and psychological altruism are independent. He rejects their arguments from imperfect belief–affect correlation, from the engineering cost of strong affect, and from redundancy. He takes seriously the fourth: hedonism depends on beliefs linking helping to one's own feelings, and beliefs can be undermined. But if those links are sticky sub-doxastic states, hedonism is as reliable as altruism, so the argument leaves egoism open. | Read |
| [NOTE-1284](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1284.md) | Self and Collective: Cognition and Social Context | Self-categorization theory's statement on the self. Personal and social identity are levels of self-categorization, equally authentic. Which category is used, and with what content and prototype, is set by perceiver readiness and fit (metacontrast and normative fit), and so varies lawfully with the comparative frame of reference. The authors go on to speculate that the self is not a stored structure at all but is generated each time. A theoretical paper; the evidence is the group's own studies, reported and not presented. | Read |
| [NOTE-1285](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1285.md) | Group-level emotions | A review of intergroup emotions theory by its founders. Identifying with a group makes it "an aspect of the self through self-categorization", so events are appraised for what they mean to the group, and emotions are felt on its behalf. Four facts: the emotion shifts with the salient membership; members converge on a group norm; no personal involvement is needed; and identification moderates the effect, the highly identified sometimes reappraising to avoid guilt. Group-based emotions predict collective action and treatment of out-groups and the in-group, and can be regulated. No new data. | Read |
| [NOTE-1286](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1286.md) | Recategorization and Prosocial Behavior: Common In-Group Identity and a Dual Identity | The common in-group identity model's authors on helping. Recategorizing two groups as one removed in-group bias in helping in a laboratory study (posters for an out-group member rose to the in-group level), and at a stadium White fans complied with a Black interviewer more when he wore their university's hat (59% vs 36%). A dual identity is another matter: White students volunteered least for a Black student who called himself a Black Colgate student, as little as for one who called himself Black, and most when he called himself a Colgate student. Empathic concern partly mediated the effect on helping (β for condition .46 to .35); attitudes did not. Sample sizes are not reported. | Read |
| [NOTE-1287](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1287.md) | A Mathematical Theory of Saving | How much should a nation save? For a community that lives for ever, with fixed numbers, tastes and motives, and that does not discount later enjoyments ("ethically indefensible", from "the weakness of the imagination"), saving times the marginal utility of consumption must equal the shortfall of present net enjoyment from Bliss, the maximum obtainable. The rule does not depend on the interest rate, and asks much more saving than usual: £300 out of £500 on an illustrative scale. A constant discount rate below the interest rate gives the same rule for a "modified utility"; one above it runs consumption down to subsistence. The paper then takes discounting as a fact of saving. People care less for heirs than for themselves, and families with different rates end divided between bliss and subsistence. | Read |
| [NOTE-1288](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1288.md) | Team Reasoning and Intentional Cooperation for Mutual Benefit | Theories of social preference can always fit an observed choice by positing a preference for it, and their non-trivial forms cannot represent trust: on Rabin's intention-based preferences, (send, return) in a Trust Game cannot be common knowledge in equilibrium. Team reasoning can, but Bacharach's version maximizes a team utility that trades members off and needs no assurance. Sugden's Schema of Cooperative Team Reasoning aims at a mutually beneficial practice, in which each member gains over her maximin payoff, and binds only when there is reciprocal reason to believe the others endorse it. A market exchange in each party's interest can then be intended as cooperation for mutual benefit. | Read |
| [NOTE-1289](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1289.md) | Second-Person Engagement, Self-Alienation, and Group-Identification | A reconstruction and defence of Husserl's empathy-based account of the "we". Truly social acts need an I–Thou relation of reciprocal, communicative address, beyond even reciprocal empathy. In it I am aware of myself as addressed, and by taking over the other's perspective on me ("self-alienation") the self–other difference stays present but is "somewhat downplayed". That is a formal, necessary but not sufficient, condition of seeing oneself as one of us. "A we, a first-person plural, is not an enlarged I." Zahavi likens it to self-categorization theory's self-stereotyping, replies to Heidegger and Schmid that the "we" can be analysed and that self-awareness precedes in-group bias, and concedes that the face-to-face "we" does not cover anonymous ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-1290](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1290.md) | Social Identity and Close Relationships: What is the Connection? | Close relationships and group memberships are two forms of social identification, "processes by which the individual self is extended to include others": the relational self personalized, the collective self depersonalized. They are distinct systems, not two routes to one need for belonging. Group and interpersonal attachment correlate only .46 (anxiety) and .33 (avoidance), and loneliness has relational and collective factors. Each level regulates opposed needs, as hunger and thirst do, with transfer between them. Relational collectivists bound their in-groups tightly; individualists identify more with large, inclusive groups and show as much in-group favouritism toward them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1291](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1291.md) | Surviving Early Childhood Trauma: Effects of the Holocaust on Survivors' Psychological and Physiological Well-Being | Four studies of one registry-drawn Israeli sample: 32 female child survivors who lost both parents, 33 matched women who left Europe with their parents before the war, and 79 daughters. Survivors, now about 77, reported more dissociation and less life satisfaction, scored lower on cognition, and had higher diurnal cortisol and an anomalous response to a laboratory stressor, the last two only in ADRA2B wildtype carriers in an exploratory analysis. Daughters did not differ on any psychological, cognitive, health or cortisol measure. Only an exploratory split found lower cortisol in daughters of more dissociative survivors. The thesis restates its promotors' meta-analyses: no secondary or tertiary traumatization in non-clinical samples with adequate designs. | Read |
| [NOTE-1292](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1292.md) | The Psychology of Rivalry: A Relationally Dependent Analysis of Competition | Rivalry is a subjective competitive relationship that raises the psychological stakes of competing with a particular opponent, holding objective stakes fixed. In student sportswriters' ratings of 71 NCAA men's basketball teams, validated by players and coaches (r = .89), half the variance (50.4%) was the particular pair of teams, not either team. Rivalry rose with proximity, status similarity, games played and, most of all, a history of even results, and history mattered more than recent form. Rivalry was largely reciprocated (r = .85 net of team effects); where it was not, lower-status teams felt it toward higher-status ones. Rival games drew bigger crowds and slightly better defence. | Read |
| [NOTE-1293](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1293.md) | Responsibility to Future Generations: A Moral Reframing Strategy for Combatting Climate Change | Felt responsibility to future generations is held by most people in 33 of 34 European countries and is nearly unrelated to ideology, age and gender. In US samples it is endorsed more than responsibility to cut one's own climate contribution, is half as tied to conservatism (r = −.21 against −.45), and predicts self-reported proenvironmentalism. A preregistered experiment (N = 3,175) found five brief interventions each raised it a little; a letter to a person born today did most, a longtermist text least, and reflecting on past generations' sacrifices raised it without raising responsibility for climate. Nothing measures how far the self extends, and responsibility is not separated from caring. | Read |
| [NOTE-1294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1294.md) | Death | The SEP survey of death. Life is the capacity of an object's parts to control what composes it; death is the loss of that capacity. Epicurus's case that death is nothing to us needs intrinsic hedonism and a narrow view of extrinsic harm. Without them, death can harm by depriving one of goods one would have had. When it harms is disputed. On Pitcher's priorism a death, or a posthumous event, can thwart desires one has while alive, and so harm one then, without backward causation. Critics answer that desires one no longer has cannot be thwarted. Luper argues that immortality need not be tedious, and that giving up desires death could thwart would cost as much as it saves. | Read |
| [NOTE-1295](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1295.md) | Reconceptualizing Individuals, Categories, and the Social Group: Self-Categorization Theory 2.0 | An insider's critique and reconstruction of self-categorization theory. Categorization into equivalence classes yields interchangeable members, not a group entity. Meta-contrast, taken as the mechanism of entity formation, is intractable (2ⁿ subsets: 9.3 hours for 25 people at 1,000 operations a second). Its prototype semantics fails compositionality. The proposed SCT2.0: self-categorization is the categorization of intentional agents; groups are holistic entities triggered by cues to collective intentionality; and relations are propositional, in a language of thought. A theoretical paper; its own evidence is under review. | Read |
| [NOTE-1296](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1296.md) | Inter- and transgenerational inheritance of behavioral phenotypes | A review from Mansuy's laboratory. In rodents, parental trauma, stress, drugs of abuse and in-utero insults pass behavioural phenotypes to offspring, in the MSUS model "up to the third or even the fourth generation"; paternal environmental enrichment passes benefits and can prevent trauma's transmission. IVF and sperm-RNA injection show germline dependence, and non-coding RNAs are the best candidate carriers. Human descendants of genocide survivors show more psychopathology; the review's own table calls these intergenerational. How a stimulus reaches the germline, and how effects pass beyond the first generation, "remains unknown". Germline reprogramming is not mentioned. | Read |
| [NOTE-1297](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1297.md) | I Belong, therefore, I Exist: Ingroup Identification, Ingroup Entitativity, and Ingroup Bias | One experiment, 48 Italian students. Writing about one's own death, against writing about reading a book, raised identification with Italians, perceived entitativity of Italians and in-group bias against Germans; the bias came entirely from rating Italians higher. Identification and entitativity are distinct (r = .59) and each mediated the effect on bias, through their shared variance; the Sobel tests were marginal. The authors propose that a group seen as a real entity lets people project themselves beyond their death, so that even dying for it can serve the self, but they do not separate this from terror management's worldview defence. | Read |
| [NOTE-1298](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1298.md) | The Afterlife (Tanner Lectures I and II) | Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures. "The afterlife" is the survival of other people after one's death. Few would be indifferent to the earth's destruction thirty days after their death, or weigh its goods against its evils. Many projects would lose their point, and in an infertile world, where no one dies early but no one more is born, even enjoyments might. Humanity's survival matters to us in its own right and as a condition of other things mattering. In that respect it matters more than our own survival or our loved ones'. Scheffler reads this as our dependence on future people, not altruism toward them, and as showing that individual valuing presupposes humanity as an ongoing project. | Read |
| [NOTE-1299](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1299.md) | Belonging to a community of European fans? European common in-group identity formation through football fandom | A quota-sampled online survey of football fans in Germany, Spain, Poland and Norway (n = 3,685 analysed). Fans identify with fan communities at three levels, club (mean 6.13/10), nation (5.57) and Europe (5.29). In a two-factor solution the European item loads on its own factor. In OLS, European fan-community identification goes with trust in European fans (b = 0.34), foreign-league viewing, positive views of fans, attachment to Europe, youth and education. It is not associated with critiques of football governance. Cross-sectional; the dependent variable is one item. | Read |
| [NOTE-1300](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1300.md) | The Significance, Persistence, Contingency Framework | The value an event E contributes through a feature F of the world is significance × persistence × contingency: value per unit of the time E adds (ΔV/ΔT), how long F lasts (T), and the share of that duration due to E (ΔT/T). Under uncertainty the factors are taken ex ante (ΔEV/ΔET, ET, ΔET/ET), which keeps the product but is not the product of expected factors. An alternative takes significance as V/T and makes contingency the sum of the semi-elasticities of significance, persistence and the probability that F exists. The result estimates the "importance" factor of the ITN framework. It is an accounting device that assumes expected-value maximisation; it says nothing about who is moved by the value it counts. | Read |
| [NOTE-1301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1301.md) | The Minimal Group Paradigm and its maximal impact in research on social categorization | A brief review of the minimal group paradigm. Groups are novel, arbitrary and anonymous, and allocations serve no personal interest. Tajfel's first studies found fairness strong but in-group favouritism reliable, and maximizing the in-group's relative advantage sometimes beat maximizing its gain. It replicated with revised matrices. It is criticized as reciprocity, as projection of the positive personal self onto the new group, and as limited to positive resources. When participants could also pay themselves, they kept the most for themselves and still favoured the in-group with the rest. The paradigm now serves mostly to study other effects of mere categorization. | Read |
| [NOTE-1302](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1302.md) | The Case for Strong Longtermism | Axiological strong longtermism: in the most important decisions facing agents today, every near-best option is near-best for the far future and delivers much larger benefits there than in the near future. The case runs through a benefit ratio. Bednets save 0.025 lives per $100. With at least 10^24 expected future beings, asteroid detection, pandemic preparedness and AI safety each buy far more per $100 in expectation; AI safety beats bednets even on an Earth-only 10^14. A stakes-sensitivity argument carries this to what one ought to do. Discounting would defeat it: a zero pure rate of time preference is "near-essential". Fanaticism is the weakest point the authors admit. They give an impersonal good as the ground and say nothing about motivation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1303](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1303.md) | Enemies with benefits: the dual role of rivalry in shaping sports fans' identity | Stadium-intercept survey at eight Bundesliga clubs in December 2014 (N = 571 after 164 fans with no named archrival were dropped); SEM. Perceived rivalry intensity lowers fans' sense of being respected by the rival's fans (β = −.31). It raises perceived distinctiveness (.27), cohesion (.20) and respect from other clubs' fans (.09). These positive effects run indirectly, almost entirely through perceived *reciprocity* of the rivalry (indirect .18–.20), and barely through disidentification with the rival. For respect from other fans the direct path is negative (−.08, ns). Cross-sectional, with a single-item predictor. | Read |
| [NOTE-1304](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1304.md) | Intergenerational Justice | The entry argues as well as surveys. Future people's existence, number and identity depend on our choices, so harm understood as making someone worse off than they were, or would otherwise have been, cannot reach them: the non-identity problem. A threshold notion of harm can: we harm someone by causing her to exist, or to be, below a normatively set level. Read as sufficientarian, in basic needs or capabilities, this grounds future people's rights, and Rawls's just savings principle is one version of it. Being weakly person-affecting, it owes merely possible people nothing, and gives no reason to prefer a flourishing future to none. Meyer fills that gap with concerns that are not rights: Scheffler's afterlife conjecture, and a duty owed to present and past people not to destroy what future-oriented projects depend on. | Read |
| [NOTE-1305](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1305.md) | Witnessing and cultural trauma: the role of flashbulb memories in the trauma process | An essay, with no new data, that adds a carrier group to Alexander's trauma process: ordinary members of a community who learned of an event at a distance. Their flashbulb memories, of where they were when they heard, let them say "I was there" and testify to what it was like. Such memories are specific to the affected community and can mark membership in it; where nearly everyone has one, speaker and audience coincide and the process starts democratically. They are inaccurate in detail but held with high confidence, and that shared confidence makes the witness "authentic". They pass to children: in Meyler et al. (2020), 89% of children nine or younger at 9/11 could report a parent's flashbulb memory, and stronger identification as American went with knowing it better. | Read |
| [NOTE-1306](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1306.md) | Review of Samuel Scheffler, Death and the Afterlife | Cottingham reviews Scheffler's book: two 2012 Tanner Lectures and a third paper given at Chicago the year before, four commentaries and replies. He reports the afterlife conjecture and its upshot, that in one respect our own survival matters less to us than humanity's. The third lecture argues that a life must be bounded, so immortality is no remedy, while confidence in our values needs others to live on. Frankfurt doubts the concern is altruistic; Wolf holds we could and should "snap out of it" and go on. Cottingham regrets that religious reflection on finitude is left out. | Read |
| [NOTE-1307](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1307.md) | Multigenerational legacies of trauma: Modeling the what and how of transmission | 422 adult children of Holocaust survivors, recruited on the web through survivor and Jewish organizations, rated their parents' post-war styles, their own "reparative adaptational impacts" and their family's history. In a path model, parents' wartime experiences, chiefly internment, were linked to the children only through the parents' victim style (stuck in the loss, overprotective, volatile), with indirect effects of .05 to .06. Post-war family milieu weighed more: living in Israel, surviving grandparents, larger families and religious continuity went with milder impacts. Broken generational linkages, rarely thinking of one's murdered grandparents as one's own, had the largest total effect (.21) and the only direct one. There was no comparison group, and the child reported every measure. | Read |
| [NOTE-1308](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1308.md) | High Risk, Low Reward: A Challenge to the Astronomical Value of Existential Risk Mitigation | On Ord's simple model, with constant per-century risk r and constant value v per century, cutting this century's risk by a fraction f is worth fv, whatever r is: halving 20% risk is worth the same as halving 2%. Absolute cuts are worth fv/r, linear and quadratic value growth give fv/r and fv(2 - r)/r^2, and cutting risk in every century gives (f/(1 - f))(v/r). In each, higher risk lowers the value of mitigation. At 20% risk a 10% cut is worth 0.5v to 4.5v. Astronomical value returns only if risk falls soon and stays very low (a time of perils of two centuries and 0.01% afterwards gives 160v). Thorstad finds the arguments for that hypothesis (wisdom, an existential risk Kuznets curve, space settlement) weak. | Read |
| [NOTE-1309](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1309.md) | Being one of us: we-identities and self-categorization theory | A we-identity is held as a group member, is at times salient, is endorsed, and varies in affective salience. Self-categorization theory explains we-identities by depersonalization: seeing oneself as an interchangeable exemplar of a prototype. Phenomenologists (Zahavi, Salice) have adopted it for the "we" in general. But close relationships, such as long friendships and partnerships, yield we-identities by mutual individualization, in which each grasps the other as non-substitutable. So depersonalization is not necessary for a we-identity. León sketches a socially extended account, drawing on Husserl and on extended-mind criteria. | Read |
| [NOTE-1310](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1310.md) | The Effects of Trauma, with or without PTSD, on the Transgenerational DNA Methylation Alterations in Human Offsprings | A short narrative review of human studies of parental trauma and offspring DNA methylation. Two parent–child studies: Rwandan mothers pregnant during the genocide and their children, with higher NR3C1 methylation and lower cortisol than a group abroad (25 and 25); and Holocaust survivors (32) and offspring (22) against 8 controls and their 9 offspring, with FKBP5 intron 7 methylation higher in survivors and lower in their offspring. Three studies of stress in pregnancy link it to NR3C1 methylation in newborns and adolescents. The authors call the evidence accumulating but preliminary, and use "transgenerational" for any parent-to-child effect. | Read |
| [NOTE-1311](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1311.md) | Economics and Identity | Puts identity, a person's self-image as a member of social categories, into the utility function. Utility falls when one's own actions break one's category's prescriptions (Is) and when others' actions do (Io); the second can be relieved, at a cost, by acting against the violator. A two-person game gives four equilibria and shows taxes and rhetoric shifting them. Applications: gender-typed jobs and their erosion after the women's movement; the socially excluded choosing an oppositional identity even with no peer pressure; and the gender asymmetry in housework, where husbands' share rises to no more than 37% however little they earn. Evidence is illustrative. The authors call identity a nonpecuniary motive and never call it self-interest. | Read |
| [NOTE-1313](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1313.md) | Mental Hoop Diaries: Emotional Memories of a College Basketball Game in Rival Fans | Twenty-three male fans, 12 of Duke and 11 of UNC, watched an archived 2001 Duke–UNC game three times in the week before scanning. Under fMRI they saw 64 clips, each ending as a shot was released, and recalled whether it went in (74% correct). The same shot was good for one side and bad for the other, so allegiance alone set its valence; fans' ratings matched their side 88.9% of the time. Good shots for one's own team were recalled more accurately and confidently and rated more intense. Intensity, not valence, modulated amygdala, hippocampus, striatum and cortical midline regions. Positive shots added dorsal fronto-parietal and sensorimotor activity. The two fan groups did not differ in accuracy or rated intensity. | Read |
| [NOTE-1314](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1314.md) | Astronomical Waste: The Opportunity Cost of Delayed Technological Development | Each second's delay in settling the Virgo Supercluster loses the potential for about 10^29 lives (10^13 if all must be biological). On a total, undiscounted view that makes delay an enormous loss. But a one-percentage-point cut in existential risk is worth over 10 million years of delay, so the total utilitarian's priority is safety: "Minimize existential risk!". On a person-affecting view only people now alive or who will exist count, and extinction is bad for what it does to them. Given a chance that some now alive live to share the cosmic benefits, safety is then very important but must be balanced against speed. The grounding is impersonal on the first view and the present generation's own good on the second. Nothing is said about motivation. | Read |
| [NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md) | Social identity theory | A textbook chapter. Social identity is the part of the self-concept that comes from group membership "together with the value or emotional significance attached to that membership" (Tajfel 1978). Categorization is always self-relevant, and the motive for a positive social identity drives comparison with out-groups; that identity serves needs for certainty, self-esteem and meaning. Low-status members choose individual mobility, collective action or social creativity by permeability, legitimacy and stability. Identification has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. At work, identification is said to matter more than "selfish concerns" of interdependence. An imagined common in-group raised children's helping of an immigrant classmate. | Read |
| [NOTE-1316](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1316.md) | The impact of place and legacy framing on climate action: A lifespan approach | 988 American adults, aged 18 to 87 and sampled evenly by age, wrote for 5–7 minutes about what they wanted future generations to remember them for (Legacy), about a place they loved and climate change (Place), or how to scramble eggs (Control). Both tasks raised pro-environmental intentions and hypothetical donations, small effects equal across age groups. The Legacy task raised an eight-item Legacy Motivation Scale, which partly mediated its effect. But the Place task raised legacy motivation too, the Legacy task raised love of nature, and with both mediators in one model love of nature carried at least as much of the donation effect. The scale's items mix wanting to be remembered with self-regard and felt responsibility to future generations. | Read |
| [NOTE-1317](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1317.md) | The Precipice Revisited | Ord updates The Precipice's four largest risks after about five years. Climate risk is down: emissions track between the two lower RCPs, and the IPCC's likely climate sensitivity narrowed from 1.5–4.5°C to 2.5–4°C, partly by our action and partly by discovery. Nuclear risk is up: the war in Ukraine, New START's coming expiry, and funding for the field halved. Pandemics and AI are mixed: Covid showed weak institutions and a brief unity, but vaccines came within a year; language models are not inherently agents and have read human values, while big-tech racing is bad and governance has improved. The book's numbers (climate and nuclear 1 in 1,000, pandemics 1 in 30, AI 1 in 10 per century) have not moved at their rounding. | Read |
| [NOTE-1318](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1318.md) | Population and Having Children Now | Narveson's late restatement of the person-affecting view, after giving up utilitarianism. Creating a person neither benefits nor harms them, since before conception there is no one to compare. But the existence of people with good lives is normally good, and a reason to create them, "contrary, perhaps" to how his 1967 and 1973 papers were read. It matters because parents and the benevolent like it and because more people benefit others. Only harm to actual persons, "alive, breathing, and acting now (or at any rate in their lifetimes)", can justify coercing procreation; possible people are owed nothing. Not aiding the poor is not harming them. The second half claims, with little evidence, that resources are created and that present and future people do not compete for them. | Read |
| [NOTE-1319](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1319.md) | A comparison of minimal group induction procedures | Two experiments (N = 42, 73) with US undergraduates compare four minimal-group inductions: false feedback on painting preference (the classic), imagined assignment, random assignment, and memorizing five names of one group with no categorization. All four gave comparable explicit in-group liking, identification and bonus-money favouritism. Only memorization gave large IAT effects of in-group preference and self-association (d up to 2.16 against the classic); the classic gave none. Implicit and explicit measures correlated weakly. Allocation favouritism tracked explicit identification (r = .37) and was carried mostly by one colour group. | Read |
| [NOTE-1320](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1320.md) | Human transgenerational responses to early-life experience: potential impact on development, health and biomedical research | A position paper of the Network in Epigenetic Epidemiology. It defines "transgenerational" broadly: any outcome in offspring of a parent's exposure before conception or an ancestor's. In the Överkalix cohorts (about 100 probands each), a paternal grandfather's good mid-childhood food supply went with higher grandson mortality (rate ratio 1.67) and poor supply with lower (0.65); for paternal grandmothers and granddaughters, 2.13 and 0.72. In ALSPAC, sons of fathers who began smoking before 11 had more body fat from 13. Against multiple testing, the authors cite prior hypotheses and coherence and grant that replication is needed. Against cultural inheritance, they cite the sensitive period in the grandparent's mid-childhood. On mechanism they stay agnostic. | Read |
| [NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md) | Existential Risk Prevention as Global Priority | An existential risk threatens premature extinction of Earth-originating intelligent life or the permanent and drastic destruction of its potential. Four classes: extinction, permanent stagnation, flawed realisation, subsequent ruination. On an aggregative, time-neutral view Earth alone could hold 10^16 future lives, so a millionth of a percentage point of risk is worth a hundred million lives. Maxipok, a rule of thumb for impersonal moral action, follows. Adams' shared project of humanity, preference satisfaction and custodial duties concur. Bostrom finds a "deficit of motivation": the good is pan-generational and public, its beneficiaries cannot pay, and moral sentiment is insensitive to scope. | Read |
| [NOTE-1322](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1322.md) | Many Labs 4: Failure to Replicate Mortality Salience Effect With and Without Original Author Involvement | Twenty-one labs at 18 US universities replicated Study 1 of Greenberg et al. (1994), in which writing about one's own death raised preference for a pro-US over an anti-US essay author (d = 1.34, N = 59). Half the labs used a protocol designed with the original authors, half built their own from the paper. With 17 labs and 1,550 usable participants, the pooled effect was Hedges' g = 0.07 (95% CI −0.03 to 0.17), with no heterogeneity across labs and no difference between protocols, under each of three preregistered exclusion rules. The expert-advised labs alone reached g = 0.08 to 0.19, none significant. The question of whether expertise aids replication went untested, because there was no effect for it to aid. | Read |
| [NOTE-1323](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1323.md) | Alvarez-Melis et al. — Hyperbolic OT hierarchy matching | Two Poincaré embeddings of the same WordNet hierarchy, from different random seeds, differ by more than a hyperbolic isometry: branches move relative to one another and pairwise distances change. Euclidean aligners and hyperbolic OT with an orthogonal map therefore fail (P@10 at most 11% across languages). Registering one space with a hyperbolic neural network trained through a Sinkhorn divergence recovers P@10 of 38–60% across languages and P@1 of 22% when matching a hierarchy to itself. The matching uses the symmetric hyperbolic distance, and nothing in it preserves the direction of entailment. | Read |
| [NOTE-1324](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1324.md) | Alvarez-Melis et al. — Structured optimal transport | Replaces the linear cost of discrete optimal transport by the Lovász extension of a submodular set function on assignments, so that the cost of a coupling depends on which assignments are made together. The problem stays convex and is a zero-sum game against cost matrices in the base polytope, solved by saddle-point mirror prox with Sinkhorn and base-polytope projections; it reduces to ordinary OT when the set function is modular. Its own example cost, eq. (12), is not concave, so the cost it defines is not submodular. | Read |
| [NOTE-1325](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1325.md) | Flamary et al. — POT | A software paper for POT, an MIT-licensed Python library of optimal transport solvers: exact transport by a C++ solver, entropic transport by Sinkhorn and stabilized variants, Wasserstein barycenters, partial and unbalanced transport, regularized transport, Gromov–Wasserstein, sliced Wasserstein and domain adaptation, with tests covering 92% of lines. It reports no experiments. Fused and partial Gromov–Wasserstein and co-optimal transport, which the record uses POT for, are not in this paper; they came in later releases. | Read |
| [NOTE-1327](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1327.md) | Yu et al. — AvAtar active OT alignment | For alignment by entropic optimal transport, AvAtar picks which source objects to send to an oracle, who names each one's true match. It scores a candidate by the derivative of a proxy utility of the transport plan (how near a permutation, or how consistent with the graphs, the plan is) with respect to supervising each possible match, averaged over matches by the current plan. The derivative is exact, from one singular positive semidefinite linear system solved by conjugate gradients. At a fixed budget of 20% extra labels on top of 20% given, it beats uncertainty baselines by up to 2.8 MRR points and random choice by up to 16, without variances reported. | Read |
| [NOTE-1328](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1328.md) | Vayer et al. — Fused Gromov–Wasserstein | FGW compares two attributed graphs with one coupling whose cost mixes, with weight α, a Wasserstein term on node features and a Gromov–Wasserstein term on structure. For α in (0, 1), q = 1 and distance-matrix structures it is a metric that vanishes exactly when a bijection preserves weights, features and structure. As α tends to 0 or 1 it tends to W or GW. On benchmark graph classification it is competitive with graph kernels, but the supplement shows Wasserstein on features alone matching or beating it on several datasets. | Read |
| [NOTE-1329](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1329.md) | Hashimoto et al. — Word embeddings as metric recovery | If text were generated by a random walk whose steps depend on distance in a latent Euclidean or Riemannian space, negative log co-occurrence over a window that grows with the vocabulary, less a term for each word, would approach the squared latent distance. GloVe, word2vec and the PMI-SVD method then have the true embedding among their optima, up to isometry and unigram terms, and a negative-binomial regression on the same relation embeds words and manifolds about as well. On real corpora the evidence for a Euclidean semantic space is a correlation of 0.75 between PMI and human similarity ratings and two nearest-neighbour statistics; the authors say the random walk is not a model of language. | Read |
| [NOTE-1330](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1330.md) | Chowdhury & Mémoli — Network Gromov–Wasserstein | The Gromov–Wasserstein distance, defined by minimizing the distortion of a coupling, is a pseudometric on all measure networks: any Polish node set with a probability measure and any bounded, possibly asymmetric, edge-weight function. It is zero exactly when the two networks are weakly isomorphic, that is, when both are images of one network that preserves weights and measures. Cheap invariants give a hierarchy of lower bounds, and the third lower bound, a transport problem whose costs are themselves transport problems, reduces to one-dimensional transport in closed form. The bounds are one-sided: networks can agree on every invariant and still be apart. | Read |
| [NOTE-1331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1331.md) | Sarkar, Mukherjee and Sato — Attention as lattice gauge theory | Under per-entity O(d) frame freedom, transports carry invariant information only around cycles, a triangle's invariants are class functions of its holonomy, and an equivariant edge update is Ψ(H)Tᵢⱼ with Ψ conjugation-equivariant: a sound conditional theorem, standard in lattice gauge theory and synchronization, whose "unique form" is a family. The untrained S4 experiments show composition doing the work and Wilson-loop routing adding 0.6–7.8 points; the 0.99 AUC is a ceiling the data's construction sets, as the paper itself computes. | Read |
| [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md) | Bodnar et al. — Neural sheaf diffusion | Bodnar et al. read sheaf diffusion on a graph as a projection onto the harmonic space of a sheaf Laplacian and ask which classes of restriction maps can make that projection linearly separate a node labelling. A symmetric one-dimensional sheaf, which is a weighted graph Laplacian, cannot separate the two sides of a balanced bipartite graph; signed maps separate any two classes; no one-dimensional sheaf separates three; diagonal maps with d ≥ C stalks, and O(d) bundles for C ≤ 2d at d = 2 and 4, separate any number. Every one of these sheaves is built from the labels. Learned from features, such sheaves give competitive node classification on six small heterophilic benchmarks. The claim that the O(d) construction exists only at d = 2 and 4 is wrong: it works at d = 8 too. | Read |
| [NOTE-1333](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1333.md) | Alvarez-Melis et al. — OT with global invariances | Optimal transport between two unregistered spaces is posed as a joint minimisation over couplings and one global linear map from a Schatten ℓp ball. Under angle preservation or whitening it reduces to maximising a dual Schatten norm of the transported cross-covariance XΓYᵀ: the nuclear norm for orthogonal maps (p = ∞) and the Frobenius norm for p = 2, which is exactly GW with cosine similarity and squared loss. Alternating SVD and Sinkhorn steps with annealed entropy solve it without adversarial initialisation. On word translation it is level with GW and behind self-learning on nine of ten directions. | Read |
| [NOTE-1334](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1334.md) | Zeng et al. — HOT multi-network alignment | Aligns K networks at once by one multi-marginal coupling tensor. The networks are first co-clustered through a fused Gromov–Wasserstein barycenter, then each cluster's nodes are aligned by multi-marginal fused GW with a cost from anchor-based random-walk embeddings, solved by a KL proximal point method. The joint objective at any tensor is the sum of the pairwise objectives at its marginals, so it bounds the sum of pairwise optima from above. On three-network benchmarks whose true correspondences are consistent by construction, it beats pairwise and multi-network baselines in pairwise and high-order hits; no experiment isolates the joint coupling from the new cost and the clustering. | Read |
| [NOTE-1335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1335.md) | Redko et al. — CO-Optimal Transport | COOT matches two data matrices of different shapes by optimizing two couplings at once, one between rows (samples) and one between columns (features), under a bilinear cost. With equal sizes and uniform weights it is zero exactly when the matrices are equal up to a permutation of rows and a separate permutation of columns, so its plans are determined at best up to the matrix's joint row–column symmetries; the paper proves no uniqueness. For symmetric matrices it is a lower bound on GW, equal to it for squared Euclidean distance matrices. | Read |
| [NOTE-1336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1336.md) | Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola — Gromov-Wasserstein word alignment | Unsupervised word translation is cast as a Gromov–Wasserstein problem between the two languages' intra-language cosine-similarity matrices, solved by entropic projected gradient (each step a Sinkhorn problem), with no anchors. It matches adversarial-plus-refinement methods on related languages trained on comparable corpora at a fraction of the cost, and does markedly worse on English–Russian and English–Finnish. The objective sees only within-space similarities, so it cannot distinguish a correspondence from one composed with a symmetry of either space; the paper does not say so. | Read |
| [NOTE-1337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1337.md) | Søgaard et al. — Limits of unsupervised dictionary induction | The adversarial unsupervised method of Conneau et al. (2018) induces bilingual dictionaries only when the two embedding spaces are alike: it fails for English paired with Estonian or Finnish, for corpora from different domains even within English–Spanish, and for spaces trained by different algorithms. A seed of identically spelled words does as well or better. A spectral dissimilarity of small nearest-neighbour graphs tracks success across eight language pairs (\|ρ\| = 0.89). The failures are partly optimiser instability (some seeds succeed), and the method tested is adversarial, not GW. | Read |
| [NOTE-1338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1338.md) | Ward & Marco — pragmatic-similarity judgments | The first set of human pragmatic-similarity ratings: 693 pairs of a spoken dialog utterance and a re-enactment of it, made six ways so that similarity varies, rated on a 1–5 slider by 6–9 judges in three four-hour sessions, two English and one Spanish, 5,532 ratings in all. Mean pairwise Pearson correlation between judges was 0.45, 0.72 and 0.66 by session. It rose with experience and fell for pairs that differ in wording (0.80 in Session 2 without them). The 0.45 the record cites is the first session's single-judge figure. A nine-judge mean at that level has an estimated reliability near 0.88. | Read |
| [NOTE-1339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1339.md) | Srinivasan & Choi — TyDiP | TyDiP gives graded politeness ratings, three crowd annotators per item, for 500 Wikipedia talk-page requests in each of nine languages. Mean pairwise Spearman agreement is 0.46 for target-language items and 0.36 for English items rated by the same bilinguals. Leave-one-out human accuracy on the binary top-and-bottom-quartile set hovers around 90%, about 10 points above an English-trained XLM-R in six languages. But annotators were screened for agreement with that classifier, and the paper's "across all nine languages" is false for Tamil. | Read |
| [NOTE-1340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1340.md) | Nicholson — The organism as a system (Weiss) | Nicholson reconstructs from Paul Weiss's writings a non-formal concept of a system: a whole that keeps its configuration while its parts vary and turn over, whose parts are produced and constrained by the network they form, and which therefore cannot be assembled stepwise or recovered from an inventory of parts. He uses it against reductionism, genocentrism, determinism and mechanicism. The critiques rest mostly on conceptual argument, analogy and Weiss's authority; only the one against determinism leans on cited evidence, and its one formal criterion, that the whole varies far less than the summed variances of its parts, is met by any aggregate whose whole is measured as an average. | Read |
| [NOTE-1341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1341.md) | Guerreiro et al. — xCOMET | xCOMET is a learned metric for machine translation, a 3.5B or 10.7B XLM-R encoder with a sentence-score head and a token-severity head, trained on DA scores and then on MQM error spans with synthetic hallucinations. On WMT22 expert MQM it reaches segment-level Kendall τ of 0.39–0.47 and span F1 of 0.24–0.32, at or above the open metrics and GPT-4 prompting of its time, and it would have won WMT23's metrics task. Its two heads agree with each other far better than either agrees with human annotators, partly by construction. It flags most injected critical errors and ranks fully detached hallucinations low. | Read |
| [NOTE-1342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1342.md) | Felekis et al. — Causal optimal transport of abstractions | COTA learns a stochastic map from a low-level to a high-level causal model's state space from samples of paired interventional distributions, given both DAGs and the map between interventions, by solving one entropic optimal-transport problem per intervention with a cost that rewards compatibility with the paired interventions and a term meant to impose do-calculus relations between plans. As written, that term depends only on the plans' marginals, which the transport constraints fix, so it is constant on the feasible set and its weight acts only by rescaling the other terms. The reported gains come from the compatibility cost when interventions are many; with few, a Hamming cost does better. | Read |
| [NOTE-1343](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1343.md) | Peyré et al. — Gromov–Wasserstein averaging | Defines an entropic Gromov–Wasserstein discrepancy between similarity matrices of any size and loss, and their barycenter as a Fréchet mean of user-chosen size and weights. It is computed by alternating Sinkhorn- based coupling updates with a closed-form matrix update that, for square loss, averages the couplings' realignments of the inputs with the barycenter weights. The algorithm is proved to keep PSD and infinitely divisible kernels in their classes; its convergence at the step size used is observed, not proved, and only stationary points are sought. | Read |
| [NOTE-1344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1344.md) | Osmelak et al. — PETra | PETra is a corpus of about 3,000 English-source sentence pairs from TED-Multi and Europarl, in twelve target languages, in which a translation adds or replaces material to make culture-bound knowledge explicit: unit conversions, entity descriptions and specifications, translator glosses. Candidates come from null alignments filtered to pairs with a named entity, and a BERT classifier trained by active learning on German and Spanish finds the rest. Measurement conversion is the largest category. No inter-annotator agreement is reported, the text points to a single annotator, and three quarters of the pairs were found by the classifier, so the labels are not a validated measure. | Read |
| [NOTE-1345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1345.md) | Singh et al. — VakyArth | VakyArth is 578 items written by four native speakers, one per language, for Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil and Malayalam, over five phenomena and three formats. Five LLMs do better on MCQ than NLI in every model–language pair, and when wrong they lean to the literal reading. COMET tracks one native rater's pragmatic-adequacy scores at r = 0.81. The translation items are not the MCQ and NLI items: in the release, 1 of 204 translation sources overlaps an inference item. So the finding that translation "does not track" pragmatic understanding compares different items. No agreement between people is reported anywhere. | Read |
| [NOTE-1346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1346.md) | Chu, Zhmoginov and Sandler — CycleGAN as steganographer | A CycleGAN trained to translate aerial photographs to maps and back reconstructs details of the photograph, such as the pattern of dots on a roof, that are absent from the visible map, because it encodes them in a low-amplitude, high-frequency signal in the map. Noise of three 8-bit levels, or JPEG compression, destroys the reconstruction; low-frequency changes do not. Any target photograph can be produced from almost any map by an imperceptible perturbation found by gradient descent, and the perturbation needed shrinks as training proceeds. The cycle-consistency loss is met by a channel the map's human reader cannot see. | Read |
